0.title: Caring for Souls: A Biblical Counseling Guide
0.overview:
This study is a practical guide for pastors, elders, deacons, and any Christian who wants to help others from the Word of God. It draws on the ACBC (Association of Certified Biblical Counselors) tradition and the work of its key practitioners: Randy Patten, who pioneered the institutionalizing of biblical counseling training; Heath Lambert, whose A Theology of Biblical Counseling gives the movement its most rigorous systematic foundation; David Powlison, whose X-ray questions and heart-focused methodology have shaped a generation; Paul Tripp, whose Instruments in the Redeemer's Hands remains the most practical introduction; Steve Viars, whose Faith Church model has demonstrated what a counseling-saturated congregation can look like; Stuart Scott and John Street, who have championed the medical referral principle and men's counseling; Martha Peace and Amy Baker, who have served women with wisdom and care; Brad Bigney, whose Gospel Treason makes idol diagnosis accessible; and C.J. Mahaney, who has kept the cross at the centre of everything.

The study is organised in four movements. Foundations (Units 1–5): why Scripture is sufficient, how to understand the whole person, how to distinguish sin and suffering, how to reach the heart, how to listen and speak. Common Struggles (Units 6–10): anxiety, depression, anger, grief and loss, burnout — each with its own unit, its own diagnostic questions, and its own gospel application. Hard Cases (Units 11–19): the situations that test every counselor — sexual addiction, eating disorders, alcohol and drugs, gambling, severe mental illness, OCD, trauma, suicide and self-harm, and domestic violence. Recommended Literature (Unit 20): the books that will take you further.

Two convictions run through everything. First: the sufficiency of Scripture. God's Word is living and active, sufficient to equip every believer for every good work (2 Tim. 3:16–17; 2 Pet. 1:3). Second: the medical principle (Street, Scott, ACBC tradition) — always refer for a medical check-up, because the body matters and physical causes must be ruled out. But refer and counsel simultaneously. Do not wait. The soul needs the Word the same day the body needs the doctor.

The goal of all biblical counseling is not symptom management. It is not merely restored functioning. It is the glory of God — that the counselee would come to know God more truly, trust Christ more deeply, and live in ways that honor Him. Every change, every step, every hard conversation is in service of this: that the person before you would flourish as a creature made for God, redeemed for His glory, being conformed to the image of His Son.

1.title: Foundations: The Sufficiency of Scripture
1.overview:
Every counseling approach rests on a set of assumptions about what is wrong with human beings and what can make them well. Secular psychology assumes the fundamental problem is psychological — rooted in developmental history, neurological patterns, or environmental conditioning — and that the solution lies in insight, relearning, or medication. Biblical counseling does not dismiss the body or deny that history shapes us. But it insists that the deepest problem is always spiritual — a disordered heart, disordered worship, disordered relationships with God and others — and that the deepest solution is always the Word and Spirit of God.

Jay Adams's landmark Competent to Counsel (1970) recovered this conviction for the modern church. The movement has matured since Adams — figures like Powlison, Tripp, Lambert, and Welch have developed a richer, more pastorally sensitive approach that takes suffering seriously and refuses to reduce every problem to simple sin patterns. But the foundation has not shifted: Scripture is sufficient. Not because the Bible addresses every technical question in psychiatry, but because it reveals the God who made the human heart and is the only one who can truly heal it.

Heath Lambert's definition is precise: sufficiency means the Bible contains everything necessary for the counselor to understand people accurately, diagnose their problems accurately, and point them toward real and lasting change. This does not mean counselors never refer to doctors — they always do for medical questions. It means they do not grant secular psychological frameworks equal authority alongside Scripture when addressing the soul.
1.text: "His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence." (2 Pet. 1:3 ESV) "All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." (2 Tim. 3:16–17 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness…
verseByVerse.commentary: The sufficiency claim rests here. All things — pertaining to life and godliness — are granted through the knowledge of God. This is not a promise that the Bible will answer every neurological question. It is a promise that God has not left His people without sufficient resources to know Him, understand themselves, and walk in His ways. The counselor who truly believes this verse will reach for Scripture before reaching for any secular framework — not because they are anti-science, but because they know where ultimate wisdom resides.

verseByVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness…
verseByVerse.commentary: Four uses of Scripture that map directly onto the counseling task: teaching (what is true — the counselor brings accurate biblical categories); reproof (where the counselee has gone wrong — honest, loving confrontation); correction (the path back — pointing to repentance and change); training in righteousness (the long work of habit and character formation). Notice the goal: complete, equipped for every good work. Biblical counseling aims not at symptom relief but at mature, equipped, God-glorifying persons.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword…
verseByVerse.commentary: The biblical counselor's primary tool is a living instrument. It is not a static text requiring expert interpretation before it can be applied — it is living and active, doing things in people as it is heard and received. It cuts to the exact depth required, discerning not just behaviour but motive, not just what the person does but why. No psychological test achieves this. The counselor who brings Scripture is not bringing their own insight; they are bringing a sword that the Spirit wields according to His perfect knowledge of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's word for instruct is nouthetein — the root of Adams's nouthetic counseling. Crucially, Paul addresses this capacity not to professional therapists but to the whole congregation: ordinary believers, filled with goodness and knowledge, are able to counsel one another. Biblical counseling is not a specialist guild — it is the congregation's calling. Every member of a healthy church should be growing in the ability to speak truth into a suffering person's life with both competence and care.

1.theology:
Sola Scriptura applied to counseling: The Reformation's insistence on Scripture's supreme authority extends to the care of souls. The church does not need a supplementary psychology to understand people — she needs to know her Bible more deeply, apply it more wisely, and trust the Spirit to make it effective. This is not anti-intellectualism; it is faith. The integrationist approach — mixing biblical categories with secular psychological frameworks as co-equal authorities — compromises this conviction at its root. Secular psychology can make useful observations about human behavior. But it cannot diagnose the heart, cannot provide atonement for sin, and cannot produce the new birth that is the only foundation for lasting change.

What sufficiency does not mean: It does not mean the counselor knows everything, or that medical care is unnecessary, or that every problem has a simple spiritual answer. It means Scripture provides the framework — the map of the human person, the diagnosis of the fundamental problem, and the direction of genuine healing — within which all other knowledge (medical, relational, historical) finds its proper place.
1.examples:
Then: Before Adams, most seminaries trained pastors in preaching and theology but referred psychological problems to secular therapists. The cure of souls — the ancient pastoral task — had been surrendered. Adams's bold reclamation was controversial but necessary: the church had the resources all along.

Now: The temptation today is subtler: not to abandon Scripture entirely, but to dilute it — to add secular frameworks as supplements, to use psychological language as the primary diagnostic vocabulary, and to treat Scripture as devotional encouragement rather than the sharp, living instrument it is. The biblical counselor holds the line not out of defensiveness but out of conviction: God's Word is enough, and in the hands of the Spirit, it is more than enough.

2.title: Understanding People: The Biblical Anatomy of the Soul
2.overview:
Before you can counsel anyone, you need to understand them — not just their presenting problem but who they are as human beings. Biblical counseling begins with a thick account of the person: made in God's image, fallen in Adam, redeemable in Christ, indwelt by the Spirit, living in a body, shaped by a history, embedded in relationships, situated in a world that both blesses and afflicts them.

David Powlison's framework is essential here. He insists that biblical counseling must engage with the specifics of a person's life — not generic categories but this person, in this situation, with this history, these relationships, and these particular patterns of thought, desire, and behavior. The counselor who listens carefully before speaking will see things that a quick diagnosis would miss.

Paul Tripp adds the language of story: every person is living inside a narrative — a story about who they are, what they need, and how the world works. Often that story is shaped more by painful experience than by Scripture. The counselor's task is to help the person reframe their story within the larger, truer story of what God is doing in creation, redemption, and new creation.

The body matters. Ed Welch's work is important here: the biblical account of persons refuses to spiritualise away the physical. Sleep deprivation, chronic illness, hormonal change, neurological conditions — all of these affect how a person thinks, feels, and functions. The godly counselor takes the body seriously without reducing every problem to a physical cause.
2.text: "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life." (Prov. 4:23 ESV) "For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery…" (Mark 7:21 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The heart is the source — not a passive reservoir but the spring from which all of life flows. What enters the heart flows into every word, decision, relationship, and habit. This is why biblical counseling is fundamentally heart-work: address the behavior without the heart and you produce behavior modification; address the heart and you open the possibility of genuine transformation. The word keep implies both guarding (protecting from what should not enter) and tending (cultivating what should grow there). Both dimensions belong to the counseling relationship.

verseByVerse.quote: For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts…
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus overturns the Pharisaic assumption that sin is primarily an external problem — a matter of what you touch, eat, or encounter. Sin's root is internal: the corrupt heart produces corrupt fruit. This is simultaneously the most humbling and the most hopeful diagnosis. Humbling, because there is no external fix — no environment change, no medication, no willpower that reaches the root. Hopeful, because God promises the one thing that truly matters: a new heart (Ezek. 36:26). The counselor who believes this will work at depth, not at the surface.

verseByVerse.quote: May your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless…
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's prayer for the whole person — spirit, soul, and body — reflects the biblical refusal to spiritualise away the physical or physicalise away the spiritual. The body matters: chronic pain, illness, exhaustion, and neurological conditions shape how a person thinks and feels. This is not an excuse for sin, but it is a context that the wise counselor acknowledges. The person who has not slept in weeks, or who is managing a chronic illness, deserves a counselor who sees the whole picture — body and soul together, as God made them.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary: The conflict Paul describes is not between body and soul (Greek dualism) but between the old self and the new — the flesh (the sin-bent nature) and the Spirit (the new creation life). Every believer lives in this tension. Understanding it prevents two errors: the moralist who expects simple obedience once the right principle is named, and the therapeutic who expects the person to feel better once they are understood. Change is neither simple nor merely felt — it is the Spirit's work through the Word, in community, over time.

2.theology:
The biblical anatomy: Scripture speaks of the human person in terms of heart, soul, mind, strength, spirit, and body — not as separate compartments but as interlocking dimensions of a unified person. The heart is the control centre: it thinks, desires, chooses, and worships. Every person is worshipping something at every moment — the question is what. The counselor's task is to help identify what the heart is truly worshipping, and to redirect worship toward the only One worthy of it.

Image-bearing and fallenness: The person before you bears the image of God — which means they have dignity, rationality, moral capacity, and relational depth that no secular framework fully accounts for. And they are fallen — which means every faculty is affected by sin: the mind thinks crookedly, the will chooses poorly, the emotions respond disproportionately, the body suffers. Both truths must be held simultaneously: dignity and fallenness, without collapsing into either despair or naivety.
2.examples:
Ed Welch on weakness: Welch's Running Scared and Shame Interrupted demonstrate the richness of the biblical account of persons. Rather than diagnosing anxiety as merely sinful distrust, Welch explores the many dimensions of fear — legitimate fears, distorted fears, fears that are both sinful and sympathetic simultaneously. This nuance makes him a trusted guide for sufferers who have been handled too roughly by less careful counselors.

Now: Before your next counseling conversation, resist the temptation to categorize the person before you have truly understood them. Paul Tripp calls this 'entering the story' — taking time to understand their history, their relationships, their losses, and their joys before making any diagnosis. The counselor who listens well for the first hour will speak far more accurately in the second.

3.title: Sin, Suffering, and Sanctification
3.overview:
One of the most important skills in biblical counseling is the ability to distinguish between sin and suffering — and then to hold them together in the right relationship. Many counseling failures come from getting this wrong: treating every problem as a sin issue (which crushes suffering people under guilt they do not deserve) or treating every problem as a suffering issue (which removes appropriate responsibility and leaves people stuck).

Powlison's diagnostic framework is essential: some people come primarily as sufferers — they have been sinned against, afflicted by disease, crushed by loss. Others come primarily as sinners — they are reaping the consequences of their own choices. Most come as both simultaneously: they have suffered in ways they did not choose, and they have responded to that suffering in ways that are sinful. The counselor must discern which dimension is primary in this moment, without ignoring the other.

Sanctification — the lifelong process of being conformed to Christ — is the framework within which both sin and suffering find their meaning. Suffering, processed with God and in community, produces endurance, character, and hope (Rom. 5:3–5). Sin, confronted with the gospel and repented of, is the occasion for grace, forgiveness, and renewed obedience. Neither sin nor suffering is the last word. Christ is the last word, and He is making His people like Himself through both.
3.text: "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness." (James 1:2–4 ESV) "Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death." (2 Cor. 7:10 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds…
verseByVerse.commentary: James does not say feel joy — he says count it joy, which is an act of the mind, a choice of interpretation. The trial is real and painful; the joy is not denial but reframing through faith. You know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness — the word is hupomone, patient endurance under weight. Suffering is not pointless. For the believer, it is purposeful: God is at work in it, through it, producing something that ease never could. The counselor holds this before the sufferer not as a cliche but as a theological conviction that shapes how suffering is interpreted and endured.

verseByVerse.quote: It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus corrects the disciples' reflex assumption — that suffering is always the direct consequence of specific sin — without qualification. This man's blindness was not punishment. It was the stage for divine glory. The counselor must hold this before every suffering person: not every affliction is the consequence of your sin. Some suffering is simply the context in which God intends to display His power, His faithfulness, and His glory. This does not answer every question, but it reframes the suffering within a purposeful divine story rather than a meaningless or punitive one.

verseByVerse.quote: We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope…
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's chain — suffering → endurance → character → hope — is not automatic. It describes the trajectory of suffering that is processed with God, through faith, in community. Suffering that is medicatedaway, denied, or borne alone does not produce these fruits. The counselor's role is to walk with the sufferer into the suffering — not shortcutting it — trusting that God is at work in the very pain the counselee most wants to escape. The goal is not the end of suffering but the maturity that suffering, patiently endured, produces.

verseByVerse.quote: Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul distinguishes two kinds of sorrow. Godly grief leads somewhere: to repentance, to freedom, to life. It faces the sin honestly, feels its weight, and moves toward God with it. Worldly grief — what we might recognize as guilt, self-loathing, or despair — faces the sin but moves away from God, sinking into self-condemnation without resolution. The counselor's task is to help the person move from worldly grief to godly grief: not by minimising the sin, but by pointing to the God who receives penitents with open arms.

3.theology:
Distinguishing sin and suffering: Not every struggle is a sin to be repented of; some are a suffering to be lamented, endured, and brought to God in prayer. A person grieving the loss of a child does not need to be told their grief is sinful — they need the God of all comfort (2 Cor. 1:3–4). A person whose marriage has broken down due to their own choices does not need only sympathy — they need honest, loving confrontation alongside that sympathy. The skill of distinguishing these is one of the most practically important a counselor can develop.

Sanctification as the goal: Steve Viars emphasizes that biblical counseling is not crisis management — it is discipleship. The goal is not to return the person to their pre-crisis baseline but to see them conformed more fully to Christ through whatever they are experiencing. This gives every counseling relationship a forward orientation: not merely what happened to you? but who is God calling you to be through this?
3.examples:
Then: Welch tells the story of a counselee who had been abused as a child and was struggling with deep shame and distorted thinking about God. A less careful counselor might have focused on her sinful responses (bitterness, distorted beliefs). Welch's approach was to spend significant time acknowledging the suffering first — validating the pain, lamenting what had been done — before gently, over time, helping her see where her own responses had become sinful patterns. Both were true; the order mattered enormously.

Now: Ask yourself before every counseling session: Is this primarily a sin issue, a suffering issue, or both? What does this person need most from me today — honest confrontation, compassionate presence, or both? Let the answer shape how you open the conversation, what Scriptures you bring, and how much you speak versus how much you listen.

4.title: The Heart: Where Counseling Actually Happens
4.overview:
Biblical counseling's central diagnostic category is the heart. In Scripture, the heart is not primarily the seat of emotion (as in modern usage) but the inner person — the place of thought, desire, will, and worship. It is the control centre of the human being, the source from which all behaviour flows. Every presenting problem in counseling — every conflict, addiction, anxiety, depression, or relational breakdown — has a heart dimension. The counselor who addresses only the surface behaviour without reaching the heart will see temporary change at best.

David Powlison developed what he calls X-ray questions — diagnostic questions designed to surface what is happening in the heart beneath the presenting problem. These are not intrusive or manipulative; they are careful, prayerful, Spirit-dependent attempts to see what the person's heart is actually doing. Brad Bigney's Gospel Treason makes the idol-diagnosis practical and accessible: what is the counselee worshipping? What are they trusting for the things only God can provide? What are they most afraid of losing?

Tim Keller (following Tripp and Powlison, who follow Calvin) identifies idolatry — the worship of created things in place of God — as the root beneath most presenting problems. The angry person is typically worshipping something they believe they must have. The anxious person is trusting something other than God for their security. The depressed person may be worshipping an approval or achievement they have lost or can never attain. The counselor's task is not to shame the counselee for this but to expose it gently and redirect the heart toward the only One who can truly satisfy.
4.text: "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?" (James 4:1 ESV) "I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you." (Ezek. 36:26 ESV)

verseByVerse.commentary: Before applying any Scripture, the skilled counselor asks diagnostic questions to find the heart issues beneath the surface. Powlison suggests questions like: What do you want most in this situation? What do you fear most? What would make you feel that life is good? What are you trusting to give you that? What would you be willing to sin to get or to keep? Whose approval matters most to you? What does this situation say about you — and why does that matter so much? These questions are not accusatory. Asked with genuine care, they help the counselee see their own heart more clearly — and they give the counselor the information needed to bring the right Scripture to the right heart issue.

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?
verseByVerse.commentary: James diagnoses conflict at its deepest level: it originates not in the other person's behaviour but in the desires warring within. The quarrelling person thinks the problem is what the other person did. James says: look inside. The desires — epithumiai, strong cravings — are the engine. You want something so badly that when you don't get it, you fight for it. The idol beneath the conflict is the thing you are willing to harm relationships to obtain or protect. The counselor's task is to help the counselee see this — not to condemn them but to invite them into self-awareness and repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
verseByVerse.commentary: Treasure reveals heart — not the reverse. The thing a person pours their resources, attention, energy, and emotion into is the thing that controls them — the functional god of their life. This is why Powlison's diagnostic questions circle around what matters most: where is this person's treasure? What are they most afraid of losing? What would devastate them if they lost it? The answers reveal the heart's real allegiance. And the gospel's invitation is breathtaking: there is a treasure worth staking everything on — imperishable, undefiled, unfading (1 Pet. 1:4). Redirect the heart there.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The most important thing the counselor must know is that heart change is God's work, not theirs. The counselor speaks, listens, questions, encourages, and rebukes — but only God can remove the heart of stone and replace it with a heart of flesh. This is the counselor's greatest comfort and their greatest humility: you are not the change agent. You are the instrument. The Spirit uses the Word through human relationship to do what only He can do. The counselor who understands this will pray more than they strategise, and trust the Spirit's work even when they cannot see it.

4.theology:
Idolatry as the root issue: Calvin's famous description of the heart as an 'idol factory' is the theological foundation of the ACBC approach to heart diagnosis. Brad Bigney's Gospel Treason makes this diagnosis accessible and practical. When anything other than God becomes the thing we must have to be okay — when our sense of worth, safety, love, or control depends on something or someone other than God — we have committed idolatry. And idolatry always produces misery: the idol cannot deliver what it promises, and the worship of it deforms the worshipper.

The Gospel as the solution: The answer to idolatry is not willpower or behavior modification. It is the gospel: the good news that God has provided in Christ everything the heart has been seeking from its idols. Security, acceptance, love, significance, purpose — all of these are found in Christ, freely, without performance. C.J. Mahaney's emphasis on the cross-centered life is essential here: the counselor who keeps bringing the counselee back to the cross — to what God has already done, already given, already secured — is doing the most important work of all.
4.examples:
Brad Bigney on Gospel Treason: Bigney describes a man whose anger toward his wife was rooted in the idol of respect — he needed to be respected so desperately that any perceived slight triggered rage. Once the idol was named, the gospel could be applied: in Christ, you are already fully respected, fully honored, fully valued by the only One whose opinion ultimately matters. The man's anger did not vanish overnight, but the direction of change became clear. He was not just trying to be less angry; he was learning to trust Christ for what he had been demanding from his wife.

Now: In your next counseling session, after you have listened carefully, try one X-ray question: What do you want most in this situation? Then listen to the answer. Whatever comes out — safety, control, respect, love, vindication, relief — is the beginning of a heart diagnosis. From there, you can bring the gospel specifically: Christ offers you exactly this, fully and freely, right now.

5.title: Listening and Speaking: The Practice of Gospel Conversation
5.overview:
Biblical counseling is a conversation — a particular kind of conversation, conducted with prayer, shaped by Scripture, and aimed at the transformation of the counselee by the grace of God. Paul Tripp's model in Instruments in the Redeemer's Hands gives four movements: love (establishing genuine relationship), know (understanding the person's story through careful listening), speak (bringing the Word to bear with truth and grace), do (follow-through, homework, accountability). Most counselors skip to speak before they have adequately known. The result is accurate theology delivered to the wrong person at the wrong time.

Powlison's principle: know before you speak. The counselor who has truly listened — who can repeat back what the counselee has said in ways that make them feel genuinely understood — has earned the right to speak. The one who jumps to application before understanding has merely demonstrated that they are more interested in their own insights than in the person before them.

Steve Viars's community model adds another dimension: the counseling relationship does not happen in a vacuum. It is embedded in the church — the congregation that worships together, prays together, serves together. The counselor who connects the counselee to genuine community is providing more than technique; they are providing the ecosystem in which lasting change occurs. Martha Peace and Amy Baker both emphasize this for women in particular: female counselors walking alongside female counselees in the fabric of congregational life is irreplaceable.
5.text: "If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame." (Prov. 18:13 ESV) "Speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ." (Eph. 4:15 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame.
verseByVerse.commentary: The most practically important verse for counselors. The temptation to answer before truly hearing is almost universal — we hear a problem that resembles one we have encountered before, and we reach for the familiar Scripture or the familiar counsel. Proverbs names this: folly and shame. The discipline of truly hearing — asking follow-up questions, reflecting back, resisting the urge to speak until you have genuinely understood — is one of the hardest skills to develop and one of the most important. The person who feels truly heard is far more receptive to truth. The person who feels processed has already closed up.

verseByVerse.quote: Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's counseling model is Christ-centred (him we proclaim), comprehensive (everyone), and dual-directional (warning and teaching). The goal is not resolved presenting problems but mature people — fully formed in Christ. Warning without teaching is legalism; teaching without warning is sentimentality. The counselor who both confronts and instructs, always with the goal of Christ-likeness rather than symptom relief, is following Paul's model. The standard is high: mature in Christ — fully formed, complete.

verseByVerse.quote: Speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The two-dimensional standard: truth and love together. Truth without love becomes a weapon — accurate, precise, and wounding without healing. Love without truth becomes a deception — comfortable, affirming, and ultimately leaving the person in their sin or suffering without direction. The counselor who brings both — genuine care for the person alongside genuine faithfulness to Scripture — is embodying the character of the One they represent. The goal of speaking is always growth into Christ, not the counselor's satisfaction at having said the right thing.

verseByVerse.quote: They sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.
verseByVerse.commentary: Job's friends' finest hour — before they opened their mouths. Seven days of silent, present solidarity with a man in catastrophic suffering. They did not explain, minimise, or theologise. They simply came and stayed. The ministry of presence — arriving, sitting, remaining — is itself a form of counsel, and often the most important form in the early stages of a crisis. The counselor who rushes past presence to explanation has skipped the most human and most pastoral thing they could do.

5.theology:
The structure of a counseling session: A useful framework (drawn from Tripp, Viars, and Lambert): (1) Open with prayer — declare dependence on the Spirit, not your own wisdom. (2) Listen carefully — ask open questions, let the person tell their story without interruption. (3) Clarify and reflect — show that you have understood before you proceed. (4) Ask a diagnostic question — surface the heart issue gently. (5) Bring a Scripture — one, well-chosen, that addresses the specific heart issue you have identified. (6) Discuss and apply — help the person see how the Scripture speaks to their situation. (7) Assign homework — a specific, practical, Scripture-grounded step before next session. (8) Close with prayer — bring everything before God together.

Homework: Randy Patten and the ACBC tradition emphasize homework as essential — not as busywork but as the bridge between the counseling session and actual life change. Homework should be specific (not 'read your Bible more' but 'read Philippians 4:6–9 every morning and write down one thing you are anxious about and one thing you can thank God for'), achievable, and reviewed at the next session. Without accountability, insight rarely becomes change.
5.examples:
The Martha model: Martha Peace's counseling of women demonstrates the irreplaceable value of female counselors serving female counselees. The issues women bring — shame, body image, relationship wounds, abuse, the particular struggles of marriage and motherhood — are often best addressed by someone who has navigated them and can speak with both authority and identification. A congregation that deploys trained female counselors alongside its male pastoral staff is far better equipped to care for the whole body.

Now: After your next counseling conversation, evaluate honestly: How much did I speak, and how much did I listen? Did I bring Scripture too early or at the right moment? Did I assign homework? Did I pray? These questions are not for guilt but for growth. The best counselors are the ones who keep learning from their conversations, continually sharpening their listening and their handling of Scripture.

6.title: Common Struggles: Anxiety
6.overview:
Anxiety is the most common presenting problem in pastoral counseling — and one of the most mishandled. Two errors bracket the failure zone. On one side, the moralizer who quickly quotes Philippians 4:6 and tells the anxious person to stop worrying because God is in control — accurate theology, delivered without understanding, that leaves the person feeling ashamed of something they already know they should not feel. On the other side, the therapist who validates the anxiety as understandable and works on coping strategies without ever addressing the heart beneath it. Biblical counseling seeks a third way: compassionate, patient, truth-filled engagement with the specific heart issues driving the anxiety in this person.

Ed Welch's Running Scared is the most useful extended treatment: anxiety is not simply sinful distrust — it is a complex mixture of legitimate fear (we live in a genuinely dangerous world), distorted fear (threats magnified beyond their reality), and functional unbelief (trusting something other than God for safety). The counselor who only rebukes the sinful dimension without acknowledging the legitimate one will not help — and may harm.

See a doctor, and begin counseling now: Some anxiety has physical contributors — thyroid conditions, adrenal issues, stimulant use, sleep deprivation. Refer for a medical check-up immediately. Do not wait for results before beginning counseling. Both happen simultaneously. The body and the soul need attention at the same time.
6.text: "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus." (Phil. 4:6–7 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Finding the Heart of Anxiety
verseByVerse.commentary: Before applying Scripture, ask questions that surface the heart beneath the anxiety. Try: What specifically are you most afraid will happen? What would that mean about you, or about your life? What are you trying to control in this situation — and why does losing that control feel so threatening? If the worst happened, what would you lose? Is there something or someone you are trusting more than God to keep you safe? What does the anxiety tell you about what you believe God is like? These questions are not interrogations — they are invitations. Listen carefully. The answers will tell you which Scripture to bring and how to bring it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The structure is precise: the alternative to anxiety is not resolution of the problem but prayer. Paul does not say 'stop being anxious because everything will work out.' He says: bring your anxiety to God, specifically and thankfully, and the peace that passes understanding will stand guard over your heart. This is not a technique — it is a relationship. The anxious person is invited not to stop feeling but to redirect feeling toward the Father who can receive it. The peace that follows is God's gift, not the counselee's achievement — which is exactly why it surpasses understanding.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be anxious about your life… Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' argument is not 'your problems aren't real' — it is a question about value: Are you not of more value than birds? The anxiety that drives the counselee is, at root, a question about whether God is attentive, whether God values them enough to be trusted with the specific thing they fear losing. Jesus's answer is a Father who notices sparrows, counts hairs, and values His children beyond calculation. This is the heart of anti-anxiety counsel: not willpower but a growing, experiential trust in the Father's specific, attentive care.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Glorifying God Through Trust
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal of counseling anxiety is not a calmer person (though that is a welcome byproduct). It is a person who increasingly glorifies God by trusting Him — in the dark, in uncertainty, in the face of real danger. Every act of choosing prayer over rumination, gratitude over dread, and trust over control is an act of worship. Help the counselee see this: their struggle with anxiety is not merely a problem to manage; it is a God-given opportunity to practice the kind of trust that honors the Father and conforms them to Christ. Homework: each day this week, write down one specific fear and one specific truth about God that speaks to it. Bring both to God in prayer.

6.theology:
Anxiety as functional unbelief: At its root, chronic anxiety often reflects a belief — not stated, but functionally held — that God is not attentive enough, powerful enough, or good enough to be trusted with what the anxious person most fears. This is not primarily a character flaw; it is a spiritual wound that the gospel directly addresses. The counselor's task is to help the counselee experience — not just intellectually agree with — the truth about God's character as Father, Sovereign, and Redeemer.

1 Peter 5:7 — casting all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you: The word cast is strong — it is an active, deliberate throwing. Anxiety is not surrendered gradually; it is actively placed in God's hands. And the reason is personal: he cares for you. Not a generic divine concern for humanity — a specific, individual care for this person. This verse, made personal and prayed specifically, can be the most powerful anxiety intervention in the counselor's toolkit.
6.examples:
Then: The disciples in the storm (Matt. 8:23–27) are the biblical portrait of anxiety. The storm is real. Their fear is understandable. Jesus rebukes the wind — then rebukes their fear: Why are you afraid, O you of little faith? He does not rebuke the fear before calming the storm. He addresses the reality first, then the heart. The counselor who follows this pattern — acknowledging the reality of what the counselee faces before addressing their response — will be far more effective than one who leads with the theological rebuke.

Now: The anxious person often needs the counselor to slow down with them before speeding up to solutions. Sit in the storm with them first. Hear what they fear. Then, gently and with specificity, introduce the God who is bigger than the storm — and who is already in the boat with them.

7.title: Common Struggles: Depression
7.overview:
Depression is one of the most complex and most important struggles the biblical counselor will encounter. Heath Lambert's A Theology of Biblical Counseling and Ed Welch's Depression: A Stubborn Darkness are the essential guides. Both insist on the same starting point: depression is not simply sinful unbelief, nor is it simply a brain chemistry problem. It is a complex condition that usually involves physical, relational, circumstantial, and spiritual dimensions simultaneously — and the wise counselor addresses all of them.

The Elijah pattern (1 Kings 19) is the Bible's most detailed case study: a man in profound spiritual and physical collapse after ministry exhaustion. God's response is instructive — food, rest, gentle questions, presence, and only then renewed commission. The order matters: God does not rebuke Elijah before caring for his body. The depressed person who is not sleeping, not eating, and not leaving their house needs these physical realities addressed alongside — not after — the spiritual ones.

See a doctor, and begin counseling now: Depression can have medical contributors — thyroid disorders, vitamin D deficiency, hormonal imbalances, sleep disorders. Refer for a full medical check-up immediately, and begin the counseling process at the same time. Do not wait for test results before engaging the heart. If there is any indication of suicidal thinking, see the hard case unit on Suicide (Unit 18) and follow emergency protocols immediately.
7.text: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God." (Ps. 42:11 ESV) "And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God." (1 Kings 19:8 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Finding the Heart of Depression
verseByVerse.commentary: Before applying Scripture, ask questions that open up the person's experience: When did you first notice this? Was there a specific loss, disappointment, or change that preceded it? What has changed about how you see yourself? How do you see God right now — does He feel near or distant, good or indifferent? What do you believe about your future? Are there specific thoughts that keep recurring? Are you sleeping? Eating? When did you last spend time with someone who loves you? Depression often involves layers — grief, loss, distorted beliefs, spiritual dryness, physical neglect — and the counselor needs to understand which layers are present before knowing which truth to bring.

verseByVerse.quote: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God…
verseByVerse.commentary: The Psalmist is doing something remarkable: he is preaching to himself. He does not suppress the depression (why are you cast down? — he names and faces it) and he does not surrender to it (hope in God — he commands his own soul toward truth). This double movement — honest acknowledgment and deliberate hope — is the biblical pattern for engaging depression. The counselor models it by acknowledging the depth of the person's experience without staying there, and by gently, persistently pointing toward the God who is the only true source of hope.

verseByVerse.quote: An angel touched him and said, 'Arise and eat.'
verseByVerse.commentary: God's first response to Elijah's suicidal depression is not a sermon but a meal. He lets the exhausted prophet sleep and then feeds him — twice. This is not a failure of spiritual care; it is a model of holistic care. The body and the soul are not separate: a person who is physically depleted cannot engage spiritual truth as readily as one who has slept and eaten. The counselor who asks 'Are you sleeping? Are you eating? Are you getting outside?' is not avoiding the spiritual — they are acknowledging the God-designed connection between body and soul.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Glorifying God in the Valley
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal of counseling depression is not simply feeling better — it is honoring God in the darkness. This means reframing the depressed person's relationship to their own suffering: not when will this end? but how can I trust God here, right now, today? The person who learns to pray honestly in depression, to receive care from community, and to hold onto truth when feeling it is impossible — that person is glorifying God in a way that prosperity and ease never could. Homework: this week, write one honest lament prayer each day (like Ps. 88), and read one promise of God's presence (like Isa. 43:2) immediately after. Bring both to the next session.

7.theology:
Depression and the sufficiency of Scripture: Lambert is clear: the sufficiency of Scripture does not mean that depression has a simple spiritual answer. It means that Scripture provides the framework for understanding and engaging every dimension of depression — including its physical dimension (God made the body; it matters), its relational dimension (isolation makes depression worse; community is prescribed), and its spiritual dimension (what is the person believing about God, themselves, and the future?). The counselor works with all dimensions simultaneously.

The difference between depression as sin and depression as suffering: Some depression is closely connected to sinful patterns — unconfessed sin, unresolved bitterness, persistent isolation. This dimension must be addressed honestly. But much depression is primarily suffering — the fruit of loss, physical illness, or being sinned against. The counselor who only rebukes never helps; the counselor who only sympathises never moves the person forward. Both truth and compassion are always needed, and wisdom determines the proportion at any given moment.
7.examples:
Spurgeon: Charles Spurgeon struggled with depression throughout his ministry, often taking to his bed for days at a time. He wrote and preached honestly about it — and his people loved him more, not less, for his transparency. The pastor who has never suffered has less to offer than the one who has walked through darkness and found God faithful there. The counselor who has known depression can say, from the inside, what the Psalmist says: I shall again praise him.

Now: When you sit with someone in depression, resist the urge to fix quickly. The person who has been in darkness for weeks or months needs you to sit with them for a while before you speak. Ask the diagnostic questions. Listen to the whole story. Then bring one truth — one — that speaks specifically to what you have heard. A single well-placed truth is worth more than a dozen general encouragements delivered too quickly.

8.title: Common Struggles: Anger
8.overview:
Anger is one of the most destructive and most common presenting problems in counseling — appearing in marriages, families, workplaces, and congregations with devastating regularity. Stuart Scott's From Pride to Humility and The Exemplary Husband both address the pride roots of anger in men with particular clarity. The consistent biblical diagnosis: beneath most sinful anger is an unmet demand — something the person believes they must have, are being denied, and feel entitled to enforce. When they don't get it, anger erupts.

The critical distinction: not all anger is sinful. God is angry (Ps. 7:11). Jesus was angry (Mark 3:5). Righteous anger — anger at genuine sin and injustice, in proportion to the offense, held without vengeance — is not only permitted but sometimes required. Most counseling anger, however, is not this. It is the anger of the heart that worships comfort, respect, control, or approval — and punishes those who threaten the idol. The counselor must help the counselee make this distinction: is this righteous anger, or is this idolatry in motion?

See a doctor, and begin counseling now: Rage and irritability can be associated with testosterone imbalance, sleep disorders, or neurological conditions. Refer for a medical check-up and begin counseling simultaneously. Don't wait.
8.text: "Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God." (James 1:19–20 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Finding the Heart of Anger
verseByVerse.commentary: Before applying Scripture, ask: What specifically triggered the anger? What did you want in that moment that you didn't get — or what did you have that you feared losing? What did you believe the other person owed you? If you are honest, was there a sense of entitlement — that you had a right to what you were demanding? What did the anger feel like it was protecting? What does this pattern tell you about what matters most to you? Stuart Scott's approach is to trace the anger back to its pride root: the person who is angry usually believes they deserve better, know better, or should have more say than they are getting. Name the idol beneath the anger gently and clearly.

verseByVerse.quote: Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: James's rhythm — quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger — is the antithesis of the angry person's natural pattern, which is slow to hear, quick to speak, quick to anger. The reversals are deliberate: the angry person must learn to override their instincts in the moment of provocation. This is not natural — it requires both the Spirit's work and deliberate practice. The counselor's homework might include a specific protocol for the next provocation: stop, breathe, ask a question, pray silently before responding. Anger management without heart change is behavior modification; but heart change without new habits is also incomplete.

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?
verseByVerse.commentary: James diagnoses conflict at its root: the desires (epithumiai) warring within. The angry person thinks the problem is what the other person did. James says: look inside. You want something so badly that when you don't get it, you fight for it. The idol beneath the anger is the thing you are willing to harm relationships to obtain or protect. The counselor's task is not to excuse the other person's behavior (which may have been genuinely wrong) but to help the angry person see that their response reveals a heart issue that goes deeper than the trigger. Addressing the trigger without the heart issue produces only temporary restraint.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Anger That Glorifies God
verseByVerse.commentary: Righteous anger — slow, proportionate, aimed at genuine wrong, held without vengeance — glorifies God. The goal for the angry counselee is not the absence of anger but its transformation: from the hot, fast, self-serving anger of the idol-worshipper to the slow, measured, justice-seeking anger of the person who has entrusted their cause to the Judge of all the earth (Rom. 12:19). This is a long journey, requiring daily repentance and growing humility. Help the counselee see that every episode of conquered sinful anger is an act of worship — a small death to self and a small victory for the reign of Christ in this person's heart. Homework: after each angry episode this week, write down (1) what triggered it, (2) what you wanted, and (3) one truth about God that speaks to that want. Bring to next session.

8.theology:
Pride as the root: Stuart Scott argues that most sinful anger is rooted in pride — the belief that I deserve better, that my judgment is superior, that others owe me deference. C.J. Mahaney's Humility: True Greatness provides the theological medicine: humility — a true estimate of oneself before God — is both the diagnosis and the cure. The humble person is not easily provoked because they are not constantly measuring whether others are giving them what they deserve. They have already placed themselves at God's mercy and received more than they could ask or think. From that position, other people's failures to give them what they want shrink to their proper proportion.

Ephesians 4:26–27: 'Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.' Paul acknowledges the reality of anger without endorsing it as a long-term dwelling place. The boundary is time: deal with it before nightfall. Unresolved anger, nursed through the night, gives the devil a foothold — it becomes bitterness, resentment, and eventually the hardened contempt that destroys relationships.
8.examples:
Then: Cain's anger (Gen. 4) is the Bible's first extended portrait of sinful anger. God's diagnostic question to Cain — Why are you angry? — is the counselor's first question too. God does not rebuke immediately; He asks. Then He warns: sin is crouching at the door. The warning came before the act. The counselor who helps the counselee identify the anger pattern before the next provocation is giving them the same gift God gave Cain — who, tragically, did not take it.

Now: Many angry counselees have never been asked what they want in the moments they explode. The anger is so familiar that it feels like a reflex, not a choice. The diagnostic questions — slow, caring, specific — often produce a moment of genuine surprise: 'I've never thought about it that way.' That moment of insight is not the end of the work, but it is a necessary beginning.

9.title: Common Struggles: Grief and Loss
9.overview:
Grief is one of the most natural and most necessary of human experiences — and one of the most poorly handled in Christian communities. The impulse to comfort quickly, to point to resurrection hope before the tears have been shed, to say 'they are in a better place' before the person has had space to feel the loss — this is well-meaning but often harmful. The God who wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35) did not skip the grief to get to the resurrection. He entered it first. The biblical counselor does the same.

Amy Baker and the ACBC tradition emphasize that grief is not a spiritual deficiency — it is the appropriate response of a love-formed heart to the loss of something or someone truly loved. The goal is not to move the person through grief quickly but to help them grieve with God — bringing the full weight of the loss into God's presence through lament, finding that He can bear it, and slowly, over time, finding that He is rebuilding what has been broken.

The book of Lamentations is the Bible's extended meditation on grief — raw, honest, sometimes angry, ultimately not resolution but faith: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases (Lam. 3:22). That truth is not the beginning of the grief journey; it is found in the middle of it, held onto with both hands in the dark.
9.text: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." (Matt. 5:4 ESV) "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit." (Ps. 34:18 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Understanding the Shape of the Grief
verseByVerse.commentary: Grief takes many shapes, and the counselor must understand which shape they are dealing with. Ask: What have you lost? (Be specific — the counselee may not have named it clearly yet.) How long ago? What was this person or thing to you — what did they represent in your life? Are you angry as well as sad — and at whom or what? Are you angry at God? What do you believe God is doing in this loss — or do you feel He has abandoned you? Is there any guilt mixed in — something you wish you had said or done? Are you sleeping? Eating? Connecting with people who love you? Grief is rarely simple. The counselor who understands its specific shape can bring Scripture that truly speaks rather than generic comfort that lands nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept.
verseByVerse.commentary: The shortest verse in the Bible and one of the most theologically weighty. Jesus knew He was about to raise Lazarus. He knew the story ended well. He wept anyway — because Mary was weeping, because death is genuinely terrible, because He entered fully into human loss rather than standing above it. This is the counselor's model: do not skip to the resurrection before sitting in the tomb. The person who is weeping needs someone to weep with them first. The truth about resurrection — real and glorious as it is — lands far deeper in a heart that has first been given space to feel the full weight of the loss.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, God of my salvation; I cry out day and night before you. Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my cry! For my soul is full of troubles…
verseByVerse.commentary: Psalm 88 is the darkest Psalm — it ends without resolution, with 'darkness is my closest friend.' It is in the Bible. God put it there. This means the cry of absolute despair, the soul 'full of troubles,' the person who cannot see any way forward — all of this is within the scope of prayer and within the community of faith. The counselor who can sit with a grieving person and say honestly, 'This Psalm was written for moments like yours,' is giving them the gift of being understood by God Himself — not just by a well-meaning human.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Glorifying God Through Honest Grief
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal of counseling grief is not the end of sorrow but grief that glorifies God — honest enough to bring the real pain into His presence, trusting enough to believe He can bear it, hopeful enough to hold onto His promises even when feeling them is impossible. The person who learns to lament well — to pour out their heart to God rather than turning away from Him in pain — is growing in the kind of faith that Job exemplified: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him (Job 13:15). Homework: read one Psalm of lament this week (Ps. 42, 62, 77, 88) and write a single honest prayer of your own in that same spirit. Bring it to the next session and read it aloud together.

9.theology:
Lament as a spiritual discipline: The Psalms are one-third laments. The church that does not know how to lament — that moves too quickly from tragedy to triumph — is not reflecting the full range of biblical spirituality. Powlison argued that the recovery of lament is one of the most important contributions biblical counseling can make to the broader church. The counselor who teaches people to bring their unfiltered pain to God, rather than suppressing it or dressing it up in premature hope, is teaching one of the deepest forms of prayer.

Resurrection as horizon, not shortcut: 1 Thessalonians 4:13 says we do not grieve as those without hope — but it does not say we do not grieve. The hope of resurrection does not bypass grief; it shapes it. It means grief has a horizon. The loss is real; the sorrow is real; the love that produces the grief was real. And one day, the one who makes all things new will answer every grief with more than we can ask or imagine. The counselor holds this hope before the grieving person — gently, in the right moment, not as an escape from the pain but as its ultimate answer.
9.examples:
Then: David's grief over Absalom (2 Sam. 18:33) — O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you — is one of the most raw expressions of parental grief in all literature. David is a man after God's own heart, and he is undone by loss. Grief does not indicate weak faith. It indicates deep love. The counselor who honors the depth of love behind the grief honors both the counselee and the God who made us for love.

Now: The single most important thing you can do in the early sessions with a grieving person is listen without fixing. Ask: Tell me about them. Tell me what you loved most. Tell me what you miss. Let the person speak. Let the tears come. Resist every urge to move to comfort before the loss has been truly heard. You will earn far more trust by saying 'Tell me more' than by saying 'They're in a better place' in the first five minutes.

10.title: Common Struggles: Burnout
10.overview:
Burnout — the state of chronic exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced effectiveness following prolonged high-demand output — is not a modern invention. Elijah under the juniper tree (1 Kings 19), Moses overwhelmed by the people's demands (Num. 11), and Martha 'distracted with much serving' (Luke 10:40) are biblical portraits of it. It appears most commonly in those who care most: pastors, counselors, nurses, teachers, parents of demanding children, and anyone who has given more than they could sustainably give over an extended period. It is both a physical and a spiritual condition — and both dimensions must be addressed.

Burnout is not the same as depression, though they overlap. The burned-out person is typically not sad so much as empty — hollowed out, with nothing left to give. The emotional detachment, the cynicism, the sense that nothing is making a difference — these are protective mechanisms, the soul's attempt to stop the bleeding. Understanding this helps the counselor approach with compassion rather than rebuke: this person is not lazy. They are depleted.

The heart questions beneath burnout are important. Often the burned-out person has been driven by something other than love for God — the need for approval, the idol of productivity, the inability to receive help, the belief that their worth depends on their usefulness. The counselor who addresses only the exhaustion without the heart beneath it will see the person return to the same pattern once they have recovered enough to start again.

See a doctor, and begin counseling now: Burnout can overlap with thyroid conditions, adrenal fatigue, sleep disorders, and depression with physical components. Medical check-up immediately, and begin counseling alongside it.
10.text: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." (Matt. 11:28–29 ESV) "He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength." (Isa. 40:29 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Finding the Heart of Burnout
verseByVerse.commentary: Ask: How long have you felt this way? Was there a specific period when you started giving more than you could sustain — and what drove that? What would have happened if you had said no — what did you fear? Whose approval were you trying to secure through your output? Do you find it easy or difficult to receive help? What does rest feel like — does it feel safe, or does it feel like failure? Do you feel your worth is connected to your usefulness? What do you believe God thinks of you when you are not productive? These questions often surface the idol beneath the burnout: the approval of others, the idol of productivity, the fear of being ordinary. Naming it opens the door to gospel grace.

verseByVerse.quote: An angel touched him and said, 'Arise and eat.' … And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's response to Elijah's burnout is the most instructive passage in Scripture on the subject. No rebuke. No lecture on trust. Just food, sleep, and the angel's gentle touch: the journey is too great for you. God acknowledges the weight before prescribing the remedy. He meets Elijah in his physical exhaustion with physical care — because He made the body and He knows that a depleted body cannot receive spiritual truth as readily as a rested one. The counselor who follows this pattern — attending to sleep, food, and basic physical rhythms before pressing into heart work — is following God's own model.

verseByVerse.quote: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus's invitation is specifically addressed to the over-burdened — those who are laboring under a weight that is crushing them. The Pharisees had added load upon load to the Law; Jesus offers a different yoke — His own — which is 'easy' and 'light.' The burned-out person is typically carrying a yoke that Jesus never placed on them: the need to earn worth through performance, to justify their existence through usefulness, to secure love through output. The gospel's invitation is radical: come as you are, do nothing, receive. This is not the end of work — Jesus's yoke is still a yoke — but it is work from rest, not work for rest.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Rhythms That Glorify God
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal of counseling burnout is not merely recovery — it is restructured life. God built the Sabbath into creation as a weekly declaration: productivity is not the point; God is the point. The person who cannot rest is the person who has not yet fully believed that God is God and they are not — that the world will not stop turning if they stop working. Help the counselee see that Sabbath is not laziness; it is obedience, worship, and trust. Every hour of genuine rest, taken in faith that God is at work even when we are not, is an act of glorifying God. Homework: identify one specific thing to stop doing this week. Not postpone — stop. Bring a written account of what that cost you emotionally and what it told you about your heart to the next session.

10.theology:
Sabbath as theological foundation: The Sabbath is not a self-care technique — it is a theological statement. In six days the LORD made heaven and earth… and he rested on the seventh day (Exod. 20:11). God rested not from weariness but as a declaration that the work was complete. His people rest as an act of trust: the work is in God's hands, not ours. The burned-out person has practically denied this — they have lived as if everything depends on them. The Sabbath calls them back to creaturely dependence: you are not the Sustainer of the universe. You never were. Rest, and let God be God.

Numbers 11 and shared burdens: Moses's burnout (Num. 11:14 — I am not able to carry all this people alone) leads to God's structural solution: seventy elders to share the load. God's response to unsustainable burden is often structural — a redistribution of responsibility, a building of team, a naming of the limits He has placed on every finite creature. The burned-out person often needs not just rest but restructuring: what is God calling me to stop doing so that someone else can do it?
10.examples:
Then: Martha (Luke 10:38–42) is 'distracted with much serving' and angry about it — a portrait of burned-out resentment. Jesus's gentle word — Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; one thing is necessary — is not a rebuke of service but an invitation to priority. Mary has chosen the better thing: sitting at Jesus's feet. The burned-out person has usually lost the discipline of sitting — of receiving, of being still before God. The remedy begins there: not with doing less, but with sitting more.

Now: Burnout in ministry is epidemic, and the church must learn to name and address it honestly. The pastor or elder who is running on empty cannot give what they do not have. A congregation that truly loves its leaders will create structures for rest, cover periods of recovery without shame, and actively celebrate the Sabbath as a communal practice — not merely a personal discipline. The healthiest churches are the ones that build rest into their institutional life, not just their personal counseling.

11.title: Hard Cases: Sexual Addiction and Pornography
11.overview:
Pornography addiction is one of the most common presenting problems in pastoral counseling today, and one of the least spoken about. The person who finally discloses it has typically carried the secret for years — often decades — and is drowning in shame. The pastoral failure mode is disgust or moralistic pressure ('just stop') that the person has already applied to themselves thousands of times without success. Neither works. What is needed is a counselor who is neither shocked nor minimising — who takes the sin seriously without treating the person as beyond hope.

Heath Lambert's Finally Free is the essential guide for both counselor and counselee. Lambert's approach is thoroughly gospel-centred: the person addicted to pornography needs not a more rigorous behavior management strategy, but a deeper and more experiential encounter with the grace of Christ — grace that is greater than their shame, and powerful enough to produce the freedom they have not been able to achieve through willpower.

See a doctor, and begin counseling now: Pornography addiction can overlap with depression, anxiety disorders, and other compulsive patterns that have physical components. Refer for a medical check-up immediately, and begin counseling at the same time. Do not wait. The soul needs the Word today.
11.text: "Flee from sexual immorality… you are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body." (1 Cor. 6:18–20 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Finding the Heart Beneath the Addiction
verseByVerse.commentary: Before prescribing, ask: When does it typically happen — what time, what emotional state, what triggers? What are you feeling just before you go to pornography — loneliness, stress, boredom, rejection, anger? What does it give you in that moment — escape, power, comfort, intimacy? What does this tell you about what you most want and most fear? Is there a pattern of shame → isolation → pornography → more shame? Who knows about this struggle? What would it mean for people to know? Powlison's principle: the specific pattern of this person's pornography use will reveal the specific idols of their heart. Do not apply generic counsel until you understand the specific heart shape of this particular struggle.

verseByVerse.quote: Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit… you are not your own, for you were bought with a price.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's argument is theological, not merely moral: the body of the believer is the temple of the Holy Spirit. Sexual sin is not just a personal failure; it is a desecration of sacred space. But notice: you were bought with a price. The same verse that names the sin carries the gospel: this body has been purchased by Christ's blood. It belongs to Him. The appropriate response is not shame-driven restraint but the grateful, worshipful stewardship of something that has been bought at infinite cost. The counselor who brings this truth — not as condemnation but as identity — is giving the counselee something willpower cannot provide: a new reason to be free.

verseByVerse.ref: The Power of the Gospel to Break Chains
verseByVerse.commentary: Romans 8:1 — There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus — is the gospel antidote to the shame cycle that sustains pornography addiction. The person typically knows they are sinning; the knowledge has not produced change because it is buried under shame that drives them further into secrecy and isolation. 'No condemnation' does not minimise the sin — it relocates the person. They are in Christ. Their identity is not 'pornography addict' but 'child of God, bought with blood, indwelt by the Spirit.' This identity — received by faith, repeated in prayer, confirmed by community — is the foundation on which genuine freedom is built. No one escapes shame by trying harder; they escape it by believing more deeply in what Christ has done.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Glorifying God in the Body
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal is not merely freedom from pornography — it is a life that glorifies God in the body. This means not only stopping sinful behavior but cultivating its opposite: genuine intimacy (with God, with a spouse if married, with accountable friends), authentic community, and the Spirit-filled life that Galatians 5:16 describes. Practical steps that must accompany gospel counsel: (1) Remove access — filters, accountability software, no devices in private at vulnerable times. (2) Break the secrecy — at minimum one trustworthy accountability partner who asks hard questions weekly. (3) Address the loneliness or stress that triggers the behavior. (4) Saturate the vulnerable moments with Scripture, prayer, and contact with community. Homework: identify the three most common triggers and write a specific response plan for each — what you will do instead, who you will contact, what Scripture you will pray.

11.theology:
Shame and secrecy as the enemy: Heath Lambert identifies shame-driven secrecy as the environment in which pornography addiction thrives. Confession — real, specific, to a real person — is the most powerful structural intervention: Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed (James 5:16). The counselor who helps the person move from secrecy to confession is doing more than managing behavior; they are changing the environment in which the heart lives. Light is incompatible with the patterns that darkness sustains.

Matthew 5:29 — radical amputation: Jesus commands the ruthless removal of whatever provides access to sin. The internet filter is not optional. The smartphone in the bedroom is not negotiable. The late-night isolation must be broken. The person who says 'I want to be free but I'm not willing to change my circumstances' does not yet understand the seriousness of what they are dealing with. The counselor must press this point with both firmness and grace.
11.examples:
Then: Joseph's response to Potiphar's wife — he fled and got out of the house (Gen. 39:12) — is the biblical picture of radical flight. He did not negotiate, reason, or linger. He ran. The person in pornography addiction must develop the same reflex: when temptation approaches, the response is physical and immediate. This is not weakness — it is wisdom.

Now: The church that addresses pornography from the pulpit, creates space for honest confession, and offers trained counseling is the church where people have a chance to find freedom. The church that never names it, or names it only with disgust, drives the struggle deeper underground — where it grows in the dark until it destroys someone's marriage, ministry, or soul.

12.title: Hard Cases: Eating Disorders — Anorexia and Bulimia
12.overview:
Anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa are among the most medically dangerous conditions a pastor will encounter. Anorexia carries the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric condition. Bulimia — the cycle of bingeing and purging — causes serious physical damage over time: electrolyte imbalances, esophageal damage, dental erosion, cardiac risk. These are not phases, diets gone wrong, or vanity issues. They are life-threatening patterns of thought and behavior that must be taken with the utmost seriousness.

While the surface behaviors differ — anorexia restricts, bulimia binges and purges — the heart issues are often overlapping: a desperate need for control in a life that feels chaotic, an identity built on body image, a profound shame about the self, a pursuit of perfection that punishes any failure. Amy Baker's Picture Perfect addresses the perfectionism and shame roots with particular insight. Both conditions are also often the counselee's way of managing overwhelming emotions they cannot otherwise process — the eating behavior functions as regulation, escape, or punishment.

See a doctor immediately — AND begin counseling now: Do not wait for the medical appointment before beginning the counseling process. Both happen simultaneously. The body needs immediate medical attention — weight, electrolytes, cardiac function, dental health — and the soul needs the Word of God at the same time. A multi-disciplinary approach (medical doctor, possibly a dietitian, plus biblical counseling) is not integrationism — it is wise stewardship of both the body and the soul, which God made as one. If the person's weight is at a life-threatening level, emergency medical care takes immediate priority.
12.text: "For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." (Ps. 139:13–14 ESV) "Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?" (1 Cor. 6:19 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Finding the Heart Beneath the Eating Disorder
verseByVerse.commentary: Take significant time to understand this person before prescribing anything. Ask: When did this begin — was there a trigger event, a period of loss, a time when your sense of control over your life was taken away? What does restricting (or bingeing and purging) give you — what do you feel in those moments? What do you believe about your body? About your worth? About what you need to be in order to be acceptable — to yourself, to others, to God? What are you most afraid would happen if you gained weight (anorexia) or if people knew about the purging (bulimia)? Who in your life knows about this? What does perfectionism look like in other areas of your life?
