The answers will reveal the specific heart shape of this person's struggle — whether it is primarily about control, shame, perfectionism, emotional regulation, or some combination.

verseByVerse.quote: You formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
verseByVerse.commentary: This Psalm is the theological counter-narrative to the eating disorder's core lie: My body is wrong, shameful, out of control, too much, not enough. God formed this body. He knitted it together with intentionality and care. Fearfully and wonderfully made — the Hebrew conveys awe, distinctiveness, extraordinary specificity. This body — this specific body, not a thinner or more perfect version of it — was made by God, is known by God, and is the object of His intentional, personal creation. The counselor does not weaponize this verse quickly or superficially. It is a truth to be returned to again and again, prayed over, saturated in — because the eating disorder's lies have been repeated far longer and far more insistently.

verseByVerse.ref: The Power of the Gospel to Change
verseByVerse.commentary: The gospel speaks directly into both anorexia and bulimia. To the anorexic whose identity is built on control and perfection: In Christ you are already perfectly accepted — not because of what you weigh, what you eat, or how much control you maintain, but because of what He has done. You are not your performance. You are His. To the bulimic whose cycle is driven by shame and secrecy: There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:1). The purging does not purify — only the blood of Christ does. The shame that drives the secrecy is met by a Savior who already knows everything and has already paid for everything. This is not a quick fix. It is the truth that, received deeply and returned to repeatedly, begins to loosen the grip of the disorder.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Glorifying God in the Body
verseByVerse.commentary: 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 — your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit… glorify God in your body — is not said to heap condemnation. It is said to give the body a dignity and a purpose that the eating disorder's lies have stolen. The goal of counseling is not a number on a scale. It is a person who increasingly relates to their own body as a gift from God, a dwelling place of the Spirit, and an instrument for His glory — to be cared for, not punished, controlled, or hidden. This is a long journey, measured in years, not weeks. But every act of eating a meal in gratitude, every moment of choosing nourishment over restriction or purging, every day of telling the truth to a trusted person — these are acts of worship, small steps of glorifying God in the body He gave. Homework: with medical team's guidance, identify one specific eating goal for this week. Write down one lie the disorder tells you about your body and one true thing God says. Bring both to the next session.

12.theology:
Control, perfectionism, and shame: Amy Baker identifies perfectionism as a central driver of eating disorders — the belief that worth is conditional on performance, and that failure to meet an impossible standard demands punishment. This is a theological problem: it is the law without the gospel, performance without grace, self-justification through self-punishment. The gospel's answer is not lower standards but a different foundation: worth that is given, not earned, grounded in the finished work of Christ rather than the fluctuating numbers on a scale.

The body's theological significance: The incarnation — God taking on human flesh — and the resurrection — Jesus rising in a body — establish that the body is not incidental to personhood. It is part of who we are, permanently. The resurrection body will be transformed but it will be a body. This means the care and healing of the physical body in eating disorders is not a distraction from spiritual work — it is part of it. Caring for the body is a theological act.
12.examples:
Then: The woman who anointed Jesus's feet with expensive perfume (Luke 7:36–50) was one whose body had been objectified and shamed. Jesus receives her extravagant act of love, defends her against contempt, and sends her away forgiven and at peace. The person with an eating disorder has often experienced their body as a source of shame and a site of punishment. The Jesus who receives the broken and shamed woman — without condition, without disgust, with genuine honor — is the Jesus who can rebuild a person's relationship with their own body.

Now: If you are counseling someone with an eating disorder, prepare for a long engagement. This is not a struggle resolved in six sessions. It requires patience, consistency, the building of genuine trust, and a multi-year commitment to walking alongside the person as they slowly, imperfectly, move toward health. The counselor who stays — who shows up week after week, who does not give up when there are setbacks — is embodying the persistence of grace. Do not go it alone: involve the medical team, the family (carefully), and the church community as a network of ongoing support.

13.title: Hard Cases: Alcohol and Drug Addiction
13.overview:
Alcohol and drug addiction combine physical dependency with profound heart issues — which is precisely why both must be addressed and neither can be ignored. The pastor who addresses only the spiritual dimension while ignoring the physical is naive; the medical professional who addresses only the physical while ignoring the heart will see the person return again and again. Begin both simultaneously.

The heart issues in addiction are well documented in the biblical counseling literature. Edward Welch's Addictions: A Banquet in the Grave is the essential guide — the title drawn from Proverbs 9:18, which describes those who feast at the table of foolishness, unaware that the dead are there. Welch argues that addiction is fundamentally about worship: the substance has become the go-to comfort, escape, and pleasure — the functional god that promises what only the true God can deliver, and extracts everything in payment.

See a doctor immediately — AND begin counseling now: Alcohol withdrawal in a physically dependent person can be fatal — causing seizures and death. This is a medical emergency. Do not tell a dependent person to simply stop drinking without medical supervision. Get them to a doctor or hospital immediately if withdrawal is a risk. Drug withdrawal also requires medical assessment. Counseling begins alongside medical care, not after it.
13.text: "Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin… So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed." (John 8:34–36 ESV) "No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape." (1 Cor. 10:13 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Finding the Heart Beneath the Addiction
verseByVerse.commentary: Ask carefully and without judgment: When did you first start using heavily — was there a period, a pain, a loss? What does it give you — what do you feel when you use that you don't feel otherwise? What are you trying to escape from, or medicate? What does sober life feel like — what is the hardest thing about it? What have you already lost because of this — family, job, health, self-respect? Have you tried to stop before? What happened? Do you believe God could free you from this — honestly? Welch's insight: the substance has become the person's primary source of comfort and relief — their functional savior. The counselor must understand what void the substance is filling in order to point toward the One who can truly fill it.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin… if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus names the condition with precision: slavery. The person who has tried to stop and cannot is not merely weak-willed; they are experiencing the bondage that sin always produces when indulged over time. But the diagnosis is in the service of the promise: if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed. Not a tentative or temporary freedom, but the freedom of sons — inherited, full, secure. This is the gospel the addicted person most needs to hear: not 'try harder' but 'there is a Liberator.' The counselor who brings this promise and believes it is the one who can give genuine hope.

verseByVerse.ref: The Power of the Gospel to Break Slavery
verseByVerse.commentary: Titus 3:3–5 is the counselor's autobiography before it is the counselee's diagnosis: We ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures. The counselor who can say this — honestly, without performance — is giving the counselee the gift of identification rather than superiority. But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us. Not because of our works but according to His mercy. The gospel changes addicts the same way it changes everyone: not through willpower but through the Spirit's transformation of the heart that has been washed, renewed, and given a new desire — for God rather than the substance.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Freedom That Glorifies God
verseByVerse.commentary: Sobriety is not the ultimate goal — though it is a necessary step. The ultimate goal is a person who no longer needs the substance because they are finding in Christ what the substance promised but could never deliver: genuine comfort, real peace, true belonging, lasting joy. This is the transformation of worship — from the idol of the substance to the living God. Practical steps alongside gospel counsel: (1) Medical supervision for withdrawal. (2) Remove access as completely as possible. (3) Build a community of accountability that is specifically aware and actively checking in. (4) Identify and address the pain, loneliness, or stress that the substance was medicating. (5) Fill the time and space that the substance occupied with prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and service — not just absence. Homework: identify the three situations or emotions most likely to trigger use. Write a specific plan for each: who you will call, what you will pray, where you will go instead.

13.theology:
Addiction as disordered worship: Welch's theological diagnosis is definitive: every addiction is a form of idolatry — the creature turned to a created substance for what only the Creator can give. This does not minimize the physical reality of dependency (the brain is genuinely altered by sustained substance use) but it establishes the spiritual root beneath the physical symptom. Address the body with medicine and the heart with the gospel — simultaneously.

Community as essential: Proverbs 13:20 — Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm. Recovery from addiction without community is rare. The person must be genuinely embedded in a community that knows their struggle, checks in regularly, provides alternatives to the isolation that sustains addiction, and reflects the grace of Christ in their response to failure. The church — not a 12-step program — is God's designed structure for this.
13.examples:
Then: The prodigal son (Luke 15:11–24) had lost everything to the ancient equivalent of addiction — reckless living that consumed his inheritance and left him in a pigsty. His turning point was not a counseling session but a memory: how many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread. The gospel reached him through a recollection of the father's abundance. And the father, seeing him from far off, ran. The counselor is the representative of the running father — coming toward the person in the pigsty before they have cleaned themselves up, not waiting until they are presentable.

Now: Relapse is almost universal in addiction recovery and must be planned for rather than treated as a catastrophic surprise. The counselor who communicates in advance — 'if you fall, call me; do not disappear into shame' — removes one of the most dangerous dynamics: the shame that drives the person underground after a failure and makes the next fall more likely. Grace must be more accessible than shame.

14.title: Hard Cases: Gambling Addiction
14.overview:
Gambling addiction is often overlooked in pastoral counseling, yet it is one of the most financially and relationally destructive patterns a pastor will encounter. The person in its grip has typically lost not only money but their family's savings, their home, their marriage, their self-respect — and still cannot stop. The shame is enormous, the secrecy almost universal, and the damage often hidden until a crisis point forces disclosure.

The heart issues in compulsive gambling are specific and worth identifying carefully: an idol of fortune and control (the gambler believes they can beat the odds, that they have a system, that the next bet will be different); often a deep anxiety about provision that the gambling paradoxically tries to resolve; sometimes a pride that cannot accept ordinary financial limits; sometimes a desperate search for the adrenaline that ordinary life does not provide. Brad Bigney's idol-diagnosis framework is directly applicable.

See a doctor, and begin counseling now: Pathological gambling is associated with depression, anxiety disorders, and impulse control conditions that have neurological dimensions. Medical check-up immediately, and begin counseling at the same time. If there is any risk of self-harm related to financial desperation, treat this as a suicide risk situation (see Unit 18).
14.text: "But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content." (1 Tim. 6:6–8 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Finding the Heart of the Gambling
verseByVerse.commentary: Ask: When did this begin — was there an early win that hooked you? What does gambling give you that ordinary life does not — excitement, hope, a sense of being special or lucky? What are you most anxious about financially or in life generally — is the gambling an attempt to solve that? Do you believe you have a system or that you can win back what you've lost? How much have you actually lost in total — be honest? Who knows? What do you believe will happen to your relationships, finances, and future if nothing changes? The gambler's belief that the next bet is different is a form of magical thinking — a functional trust in luck or fate rather than God. Naming this gently and specifically opens the door to the gospel's real offer: a provision and a future that do not depend on chance.

verseByVerse.quote: Godliness with contentment is great gain…
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's definition of 'great gain' is the antithesis of the gambler's pursuit. We brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out — the gambler is playing with borrowed chips, on borrowed time, in a world they did not create and will not control. The alternative Paul offers is not poverty but contentment with godliness — a deep, settled sufficiency that does not require the jackpot because it has already received the inheritance. The counselor's task is to help the gambler see that what they are seeking at the casino — security, significance, a feeling that the future is safe — is already theirs in Christ, freely and without risk.

verseByVerse.ref: The Power of the Gospel to Produce Contentment
verseByVerse.commentary: Philippians 4:11–13 — I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content — is Paul's testimony of a grace-won peace that the gambler most deeply needs but is seeking in entirely the wrong place. I can do all things through him who strengthens me — including living within ordinary financial means, without the thrill of the bet, without the fantasy of the jackpot. Contentment is learned, Paul says — not given instantly but developed through the practice of trust in specific situations of scarcity. This is the long work of counseling: teaching the gambler to find their sufficiency in Christ, one ordinary day at a time, one unglamorous provision at a time.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Glorifying God in Financial Faithfulness
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal of counseling gambling is not merely debt management or behavioral abstinence — it is a person who increasingly glorifies God through faithful stewardship of what they have been given. This means addressing the idol (fortune, control, excitement), not just the behavior. Practical steps: (1) Total transparency about finances with spouse or accountability partner. (2) Remove all access — no gambling venues, apps, or online accounts; this must be structural, not merely intended. (3) Address the debts honestly — with a trusted financial advisor if necessary. (4) Address the underlying anxiety or boredom that gambling was medicating. (5) Develop a theology of work and provision — that God provides through faithful work and wise stewardship, not chance. Homework: this week, write down every financial decision you make and one thing you thanked God for in each one. Bring the list to the next session.

14.theology:
The theology of contentment vs. the idol of fortune: Gambling represents the practical denial of several key truths: that God is our Provider (Phil. 4:19), that wealth sought by shortcuts shrinks (Prov. 13:11), that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Tim. 6:10), and that anxious pursuit of security through any means other than trust in God is functional atheism. The counselor who addresses these theological roots — not just the behavior — is doing the deepest and most lasting work.

Matthew 6:25–34 on anxiety and provision: The gambling addiction often medicates a deeper anxiety about the future — will there be enough? Will I be okay? Jesus's answer is not 'the numbers will work out' but 'your heavenly Father knows what you need.' The counselor helps the person move from trusting luck to trusting the Father — a profound reorientation of the heart that produces both freedom from gambling and a new relationship to money and provision.
14.examples:
Then: Proverbs speaks repeatedly of the folly of seeking wealth through shortcuts (Prov. 13:11; 28:22). The wisdom literature understood that sustainable provision comes through faithful work, honest dealing, and patient accumulation — not through chance. The gambler is repeating the ancient folly of those who pursue riches dishonestly and end up in poverty. Wisdom, by contrast, is the patient, God-trusting, ordinary-faithfulness path that ends in genuine flourishing.

Now: The family damage from gambling addiction is often enormous and requires specific attention. Spouses and children who have been lied to, whose savings have been stolen, whose trust has been repeatedly broken, need their own pastoral care alongside the gambler's counseling. The counselor who works with the whole family system — not just the identified patient — is addressing the full scope of what the addiction has done.

15.title: Hard Cases: Severe Mental Illness
15.overview:
Severe mental illness — schizophrenia, psychosis, severe bipolar disorder with psychotic features — is among the most challenging situations a pastor will face, and among the most important to handle with humility and care. The person who is hearing voices, holding fixed false beliefs (delusions), or has lost touch with reality is not primarily in need of biblical counseling in that acute moment. They are in need of a psychiatrist. The pastor's role here is not primary treatment but faithful, long-term presence alongside medical care.

This is not a retreat from the sufficiency of Scripture — it is an application of it. Scripture teaches that we are embodied creatures, that the fall corrupted all of creation including the brain, and that the body needs medicine as the soul needs the Word. These are complementary truths, not competing ones. The biblical counselor who walks alongside the psychiatrist — providing community, pastoral presence, biblical identity, hope, and support for the family — is doing irreplaceable work that no medication can do.

See a doctor immediately — AND begin pastoral presence now: Acute psychosis requires emergency psychiatric evaluation. Do not wait. At the same time, do not withdraw. Begin pastoral presence — visiting, praying, maintaining relationship — alongside the medical care. The two run simultaneously. The church's presence is not contingent on the medical situation being resolved.
15.text: "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit." (Ps. 34:18 ESV) "A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench." (Isa. 42:3 ESV)

verseByVerse.commentary: In severe mental illness, the diagnostic questions are directed as much toward the family as toward the person themselves (who may not be accessible in an acute episode). Ask family members: How long has this been happening? Has there been a previous diagnosis? Is the person currently under psychiatric care and on medication? Are they taking their medication consistently? Is there a crisis plan in place? What does this person's best functioning look like — what can they do, what do they enjoy, what connects them to God and to others? What does the family need right now? For the person themselves, in a stable period: How are you feeling about your diagnosis? What do you find most helpful? What do you believe God thinks of you in the midst of this? What gives you hope?

verseByVerse.quote: The creation was subjected to futility… the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The fall corrupted the whole creation — including the brain. Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and psychosis are not spiritual failures or divine punishments; they are part of creation's groaning under the weight of the fall. The person with severe mental illness is suffering under a brokenness they did not choose and cannot simply repent their way out of. The counselor who understands this will not demand spiritual performance from someone whose brain is not functioning normally, and will not interpret the symptoms as evidence of inadequate faith. They will sit with the person in the brokenness with the same compassion with which God sits with a groaning creation.

verseByVerse.quote: A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus's pastoral policy toward the fragile and barely-functioning. The person with severe mental illness is the bruised reed — barely standing, fragile, close to breaking. The faintly burning wick — dimly lit, more smoke than flame. Jesus does not break or quench them. He tends them with patient, persevering care. The pastor who visits the psychiatric ward, who maintains relationship through hospitalizations, who treats the person with severe mental illness with dignity and genuine pastoral care, is embodying the character of the One who tends bruised reeds.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Faithful Presence That Glorifies God
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal in severe mental illness is not cure — though the counselor prays for it. It is faithful presence: the church surrounding the person and their family with consistent, non-abandoning love that reflects the character of God. Even in the most severe cases, there are contributions the church uniquely can make: affirming the person's identity in Christ when their own mind cannot reliably do so, maintaining community and belonging, supporting the family who are often exhausted and isolated, and holding hope when the person cannot hold it themselves. This is the church at its most profound — present in the darkest places, for as long as it takes, to the glory of God. Identify one specific way to increase pastoral contact with this person or family this week — a visit, a meal, a phone call. Do it.

15.theology:
Body and soul in severe mental illness: Ed Welch's Blame It on the Brain? provides the essential theological framework: the brain is an organ; like any organ, it can malfunction due to the fall. Malfunctioning brains affect thought, emotion, and perception — but they do not affect the person's standing before God, their identity in Christ, or the reality of God's love for them. The counselor holds both truths simultaneously: this person needs medical help for their brain, and this person needs pastoral care for their soul. Neither truth cancels the other.

The family's needs: Caring for a family member with severe mental illness is one of the most exhausting and isolating experiences a person can face. The church's care for the family — practical help, respite, prayer, honest acknowledgment of the difficulty — is as important as its care for the person who is ill. The counselor who sees the whole family system and attends to it is doing the full scope of pastoral care.
15.examples:
Then: Nebuchadnezzar's madness (Dan. 4:28–37) is the Bible's most dramatic account of what looks like severe mental illness — living like an animal, unable to relate to human society. God's purpose in it was sovereign and redemptive: at the end of the period, Nebuchadnezzar's reason returned and he praised the Most High. This does not mean all severe mental illness resolves this way — but it does mean that God is not absent from the worst episodes of mental breakdown, and His purposes are not frustrated by them.

Now: Every congregation should have a plan before a psychiatric crisis arrives. Who do we call? What is the process? Who will accompany the person to the hospital? Who will support the family? Who will maintain pastoral contact during hospitalization? The church that has thought through these questions before the crisis is far better equipped to respond faithfully than the one that scrambles in the moment.

16.title: Hard Cases: OCD and Intrusive Thoughts
16.overview:
Few people in a congregation suffer more quietly and more alone than those tormented by intrusive thoughts. These are unwanted, involuntary thoughts that horrify the person who has them — thoughts of harming someone they love, blasphemous thoughts about God, sexual thoughts about inappropriate people, violent images that arrive without invitation. Crucially: the person is not planning to act on these thoughts. They are desperately trying to make them stop. And the harder they try, the louder the thoughts become — because OCD feeds on resistance.

In scrupulosity — the religious form of OCD — the person cannot shake the conviction that they have committed an unforgivable sin, or that their intrusive thoughts mean they have blasphemed the Holy Spirit, or that God has rejected them. This is one of the most pastorally treacherous territories: the counselor who responds to the scrupulous person's fears with simple reassurance ('you're fine') triggers the next cycle; but the counselor who takes every expressed fear at face value and provides extensive theological explanations also feeds the compulsive seeking of reassurance that sustains the disorder.

See a doctor, and begin counseling now: OCD has neurological components and responds to specific treatments (ERP — Exposure and Response Prevention — alongside pastoral care). Refer for psychiatric evaluation immediately. Begin counseling simultaneously. The two work together, not sequentially.
16.text: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." (Rom. 8:1 ESV) "We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ." (2 Cor. 10:5 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Understanding the Shape of the OCD
verseByVerse.commentary: Ask carefully: Can you describe a typical intrusive thought — what does it say, and when does it typically come? How do you respond when it comes — do you try to suppress it, argue against it, seek reassurance, or perform some mental or physical ritual to neutralize it? How long have these thoughts been happening? Do they cluster around particular fears — harming someone, blasphemy, contamination, sexual sin? Do you seek reassurance from others — and does the reassurance help, or only briefly? Do you believe the thoughts mean something about who you are or what you want? Understanding the specific OCD cycle (obsession → anxiety → compulsion → temporary relief → return of obsession) is essential before any intervention. Crucially: these thoughts are not the person's desires. They are the opposite of desire.

verseByVerse.quote: Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.
verseByVerse.commentary: This passage is the pastoral key to intrusive thoughts. Sin begins with desire — the heart's willing movement toward what it wants. Intrusive thoughts are not desires; they are the opposite of desire. The person tormented by violent or blasphemous thoughts does not desire the content — they are horrified by it. James 1:14–15 does not apply to the involuntary intrusion — it applies to the willful entertaining. The counselor who helps the person understand this distinction — clearly, repeatedly — is removing one of the heaviest burdens: the false belief that having the thought means wanting it, and wanting it means being it. This is not so. The thought is not the sin.

verseByVerse.quote: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: For the scrupulous person, this verse must be applied with surgical precision and repeated patience. No condemnation — not 'reduced condemnation,' not 'conditional condemnation,' not 'condemnation suspended pending your performance.' None. The counselor does not add conditions that Paul does not add. The scrupulous person's OCD will always find another sin to worry about, another reassurance to seek. The pastoral response is not to provide an exhaustive theological reassurance (which feeds the cycle) but to return, gently and firmly, to the anchor: You are in Christ. That is settled. Return to Christ, not to the fear.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Freedom That Glorifies God
verseByVerse.commentary: Taking thoughts captive (2 Cor. 10:5) in the OCD context means not suppressing or fighting the intrusive thought (which intensifies it) but: notice it, name it (that is an intrusive thought, not a desire, not a sin), and redirect attention toward Christ — not toward arguing against the thought, not toward reassurance-seeking, but toward active engagement with truth. Practical counsel: (1) Do not seek reassurance — from the counselor, from Scripture used compulsively, or from other people — when an intrusive thought strikes. (2) Practice tolerating the anxiety without the compulsion. (3) Return to a settled engagement with Christ rather than a reactive engagement with the thought. The goal is a person who can hold an intrusive thought loosely — acknowledging it without being controlled by it — and whose identity is built on their standing in Christ, not on the absence of difficult thoughts. Homework: when the next intrusive thought comes, write it down, write 'this is a thought, not a desire, not a sin,' and write one truth about who you are in Christ. Do not seek reassurance. Bring the written record to the next session.

16.theology:
The pastoral danger of the reassurance cycle: The scrupulous person will often come to the counselor seeking theological reassurance about a specific sin or thought. Providing extensive reassurance feels like pastoral care but actually feeds the OCD cycle: the reassurance provides temporary relief, which reinforces the seeking behavior, which intensifies the next episode. The more therapeutically faithful response — learned from ERP — is to provide general, brief reassurance while declining to engage with the specific fear in detail. This is counterintuitive but important.

The distinction between OCD thoughts and temptation: Every counselor working with OCD must understand this: the intrusive thought that horrifies the person is categorically different from the temptation that the sinful flesh entertains. One is involuntary and ego-dystonic (contrary to the person's desires); the other is voluntary and ego-syntonic (in line with the flesh's desires). Confusing them does enormous damage. The counselor who treats OCD thoughts as evidence of spiritual failure has misdiagnosed the situation and will add suffering to suffering.
16.examples:
Then: Martin Luther's scrupulosity is well-documented — his fear of never having confessed adequately, his terror that he had sinned beyond God's reach. His confessor von Staupitz famously told him to go commit a real sin worth confessing. This was not dismissal — it was a pastoral instinct to break the cycle of endless self-examination and redirect Luther toward the cross. The Reformation's central discovery — justification by faith alone — was in part Luther's escape from the prison of scrupulosity. The person with OCD today is often living in Luther's pre-Reformation darkness, seeking a peace that willpower and confession cannot provide. The gospel is the only exit.

Now: Working with OCD requires the counselor to learn a different pastoral reflex: instead of reassuring, redirect. Instead of answering the specific theological fear, point to the settled reality of Christ. This feels less pastoral at first — it seems harsh not to answer the question. But the person who has found that Christ is sufficient even when the fear is unresolved is more genuinely helped than the person who has received one more round of reassurance that will satisfy only until the next intrusive thought arrives.

17.title: Hard Cases: Trauma and Sexual Abuse
17.overview:
Trauma — and sexual abuse in particular — requires from the pastoral counselor a posture before it requires a technique: slowness, gentleness, absolute trustworthiness, and a willingness to listen without fixing. The person who has been sexually abused has had their bodily autonomy violated, their trust shattered (often by someone known and trusted), and their sense of the world as safe fundamentally destroyed. They may have been carrying this for years or decades in silence. The pastor who receives this disclosure has a moment of enormous importance: their response in the next five minutes will either confirm that it is finally safe to speak, or confirm the person's deepest fear that no one can be trusted with this.

Go slowly. Listen far more than you speak. Do not minimize, spiritualize prematurely, or rush toward forgiveness before the person has been truly heard. The abused person already carries enough false guilt — they have often been told or have concluded that it was somehow their fault. The counselor's first and most essential task is to say, clearly and compassionately, the thing they most need to hear: What was done to you was wrong. It was not your fault. You are not alone.

See a doctor, and begin counseling now: Trauma has neurological components — the brain is genuinely affected by severe trauma, particularly repeated childhood trauma. Refer for a medical assessment, particularly if there are physical symptoms, sleep disorders, or dissociation. Begin counseling simultaneously. And follow mandatory reporting laws: if a child is currently at risk, report to authorities immediately.
17.text: "He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives… to comfort all who mourn." (Isa. 61:1–3 ESV) "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin." (Heb. 4:15 ESV)

verseByVerse.commentary: Before asking anything, establish safety: I'm grateful you've trusted me with this. There's no pressure to share more than you're ready to share. I'm going to listen. Then, slowly and only as trust develops: When did this happen — how old were you? Was this a one-time event or did it happen repeatedly? Who did this? Are you safe now — is there any current risk? Have you ever spoken about this to anyone before? What has made it hardest to speak about — fear, shame, not wanting to upset people, not being believed? What do you believe about yourself because of what happened? What do you believe about God — does He feel near or distant, trustworthy or absent? Take weeks, not one session, to understand the full picture. The relationship of safety must precede the application of truth.

verseByVerse.quote: He has not despised or scorned the suffering of the afflicted one; he has not hidden his face from him but has listened to his cry for help.
verseByVerse.commentary: God does not despise the suffering of the abused person. He does not turn His face away in disgust or embarrassment. He has not hidden His face — He has listened. This is the word for the person who fears that God looks away from what was done to them, or that their suffering is too shameful for His attention. God's response to the cry of the abused is attention, not aversion. The counselor who communicates this — not by quoting the verse quickly, but by their own attentive, non-turning-away presence — is embodying what they are claiming about God.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses… Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace.
verseByVerse.commentary: The incarnation means the Son of God knows, from the inside, what violation and suffering feel like. He was betrayed by a trusted companion. He was stripped. He was publicly shamed. He cried out in abandonment. He is not a distant, unaffected sovereign dispensing comfort from a safe distance — He entered the suffering fully. The trauma survivor who encounters this truth — that their High Priest has walked through the worst — has found in Christ not just a sympathizer but a companion who has been there and survived it, and who has opened the way for them to draw near to God with their wounds rather than hiding them.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Healing That Glorifies God
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal is not the absence of pain — it is a person who can bring their full history into God's presence, find that He receives it without flinching, and gradually be rebuilt into someone who is defined not by what was done to them but by who they are in Christ. Isaiah 61:3 speaks of 'beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise instead of a faint spirit' — this is not a quick exchange but a slow, Spirit-worked transformation. The person who moves through trauma toward a deep trust in the God who heals the brokenhearted glorifies Him in a way that easy lives cannot. Forgiveness of the abuser — where it becomes possible — is a long-term goal, held in patient hope, never rushed or demanded. It is God's gift at the right time, not a prerequisite for healing.

17.theology:
Shame and identity: Sexual abuse almost universally produces shame — not the godly sorrow that leads to repentance, but the toxic shame that says I am damaged, defiled, permanently broken. This shame is a lie, and it is the counselor's task to speak truth against it — patiently, persistently, specifically. The person's identity in Christ is not diminished by what was done to them. They are still made in God's image, loved by Christ, purchased by His blood, and indwelt by the Spirit. What was done to the body does not touch what God has done to the soul.

Mandatory reporting: Every counselor must know their legal obligations regarding the reporting of current child abuse. If a child is currently at risk — if abuse is ongoing or if another child could be in danger — the counselor has both a legal and a moral obligation to report to the appropriate authorities. This is not a betrayal of confidentiality; it is the protection of the vulnerable that Psalm 82:3–4 commands.
17.examples:
Then: Tamar's story (2 Sam. 13) is the Bible's most painful account of sexual abuse within a family — the violation, the aftermath, the desolate silence. What strikes the careful reader is what does not happen: no one stands with Tamar, no one speaks for her, no one pursues justice. The silence of David and the action of Absalom produce more tragedy. The church that does what the palace failed to do — that stands with the abused, speaks for the vulnerable, and pursues justice — is being the community God designed it to be.

Now: The counselor who works with trauma must attend to their own soul. Vicarious trauma — the accumulation of absorbing others' worst stories — is real and must be managed: regular supervision or consultation, personal rhythms of prayer and Sabbath, honest relationships with people who know what you carry. The counselor who is running on empty cannot be present to the suffering person in the way they need. Sustaining yourself is not selfishness — it is the prerequisite for sustained faithfulness.

18.title: Hard Cases: Suicide and Self-Harm
18.overview:
Suicide is the pastoral emergency above all others. A person who is actively suicidal is in immediate danger of death, and the pastor's response may be the difference between life and death. This is not hyperbole — it is the weight that pastoral care in this area carries, and the counselor must be prepared before the crisis arrives.

Emergency protocol — apply immediately if active risk: If a person discloses active suicidal intent with a plan and means, do not leave them alone. Call emergency services (911) or take them to the emergency room immediately. Do not promise confidentiality about active suicidal intent. Remove access to means if possible (firearms are the most lethal method — ask directly about them). Contact family or a trusted person to stay with them. Follow up every day until the crisis has passed and professional support is in place. This is not a situation for a counseling appointment next week.

Self-harm (cutting, burning, hitting) without suicidal intent is different but also serious — it is typically a way of managing overwhelming emotional pain by externalizing it. It requires a medical assessment (wounds, infection risk, severity) and ongoing counseling. Begin both immediately.
18.text: "Neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord." (Rom. 8:38–39 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Assessing Risk and Understanding the Pain
verseByVerse.commentary: Ask directly — research shows that asking about suicide does not increase risk; it decreases it by opening the door: Are you thinking about ending your life? Do you have a plan? Do you have access to the means? Have you attempted before? Is there anything keeping you from acting on these thoughts right now? These are not questions to ask timidly or to avoid. After assessing immediate risk, understand the pain: What has brought you to this point? What feels unlivable? What do you believe will happen to the people you love if you die — and does that matter to you? What do you believe about God right now — where is He in this? Is there any part of you that wants to be here, that wants things to be different? The part that wants to live is the part the counselor must reach.

verseByVerse.quote: He asked that he might die, saying, 'It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life.' … An angel touched him and said, 'Arise and eat.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Elijah — prophet of fire, man of extraordinary faith — sits under a tree and asks to die. God's response is not rebuke but care: food, rest, the angel's gentle touch. Before any theology, before any commission, before any word about the future — food and sleep. God meets the suicidal prophet in his physical exhaustion with physical care. The counselor does the same: attend to the immediate physical needs (sleep, safety, food) before pressing into the spiritual questions. And note what God does not do: He does not rebuke Elijah for his despair. He does not call it unbelief and command him to repent. He meets him where he is.

verseByVerse.ref: The Power of the Gospel in the Darkest Place
verseByVerse.commentary: Romans 8:38–39 — neither death nor life… will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus — is the gospel's answer to the suicidal person's deepest fear: that they have put themselves beyond reach. Not the death they are contemplating, not the life that feels unlivable, not the depth of the despair they are in — nothing in all creation. The love of God in Christ is not contingent on the person's stability, performance, or faith-level. It is the love of One who has already gone into the darkest place — the cross, the tomb — and come out the other side. The person who is in the darkest place is precisely where this love meets them.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Staying Alive to Glorify God
verseByVerse.commentary: In the acute phase, the goal is one thing: staying alive. Everything else — theology, long-term counseling goals, understanding the heart issues — is secondary to the immediate goal of keeping the person safe. Once safety is established and maintained, the longer goal emerges: helping the person discover that life, even painful life, can be lived to the glory of God — that they have a story yet to be written, people yet to love, and a God who has not finished with them. The person who survives a suicidal crisis and comes to trust God through the darkness often becomes one of the most powerful witnesses to His faithfulness that a congregation has. The goal is not to eliminate pain but to live through it in the presence of God. Homework (in the recovery phase): write one reason to be alive this week. It can be small. Bring it.

18.theology:
Suicide and Christian theology: The church has historically treated suicide as a serious sin — the taking of a life that belongs to God. This theological conviction must be held with pastoral wisdom: a person in suicidal crisis is not primarily in need of a lecture on the sinfulness of suicide. They are in need of care, presence, and the gospel's promise that life is not hopeless. The theological truth that life belongs to God is better conveyed by a community that stays close and refuses to abandon the person than by a statement delivered in the middle of a crisis.

Self-harm without suicidal intent: Self-harm is typically a coping mechanism for overwhelming emotional pain — the person has discovered that physical pain provides a temporary release from unbearable internal pain. The counselor addresses both: the immediate physical care (wounds, medical assessment), the underlying pain (what is so overwhelming that this seems like the only relief?), and the gospel's offer of a different kind of relief — the peace that surpasses understanding (Phil. 4:7) that does not require self-harm to access.
18.examples:
Then: Psalm 88 ends in darkness: 'darkness is my closest friend.' It is in the Bible. This means the cry of absolute despair — the life that sees no light — is within the scope of prayer and within the community of faith. The person in suicidal darkness who can pray Psalm 88 is doing something remarkable: bringing their despair to God rather than away from Him. The counselor who can sit with that prayer — who does not need to resolve it, who can be present in the dark — is offering something more valuable than any technique.

Now: Every congregation should develop a pastoral response plan for suicidal crises before one occurs: Who is trained to assess? Who is available 24/7? What is the relationship with local emergency services? Who provides follow-up after a hospitalization? The church that has thought through these questions is far better equipped to stay close when the darkness comes.

19.title: Hard Cases: Domestic Violence and Abuse
19.overview:
Domestic violence and abuse is one of the most dangerous and most frequently mishandled situations in the church. It is dangerous because abusers are often charming, church-active, and skilled at presenting themselves as the victim. It is mishandled because pastors, trained in the theology of reconciliation, often apply marriage-preservation principles to a situation that requires safety-first principles — and send an abused spouse back into danger with an admonition to pray more or be more submissive.

The first and non-negotiable priority is the safety of the abused person and any children. Before anything else — before counseling, before marriage restoration, before theological discussion — the immediate question is: Is this person safe? If not, ensure their safety first. This may mean helping them access a safe house, informing them of their legal options, and — if children are at risk — making the required mandatory report to child protective services.

Domestic abuse is not a conflict problem requiring conflict resolution. It is a power and control problem requiring accountability and protection. Do not bring the abuser and the abused person together for joint counseling until the abuser has demonstrated sustained, verified repentance over a significant period. Premature couples counseling in an abusive relationship gives the abuser new information to weaponize and new leverage to use.
19.text: "Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked." (Ps. 82:4 ESV) "He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Mic. 6:8 ESV)

verseByVerse.ref: Diagnostic Questions — Assessing Safety and Understanding the Situation
verseByVerse.commentary: Ask privately, without the suspected abuser present: Are you safe at home? Has your partner ever hit you, choked you, or threatened to hurt you or the children? Has he controlled your money, your relationships, your movements? Has he threatened to hurt himself or others if you leave? Do you feel free to come and go as you please, to see your friends and family, to disagree with him? Are the children safe? Have you ever felt afraid of him? The Duluth Model's power and control wheel is a useful diagnostic framework — not as a secular authority but as a practical tool for identifying patterns. The abused person often minimizes, explains away, or protects the abuser. The counselor creates safety for the truth to emerge by asking specific questions without judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: What does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?
verseByVerse.commentary: Justice — mishpat — is the first requirement named. Not peace, not reconciliation, not harmony — justice. In the context of domestic abuse, justice means naming what is happening accurately (abuse, not 'conflict'), protecting the vulnerable from further harm, holding the powerful accountable, and not restoring a relationship that is not yet safe. The pastor who prioritizes marriage preservation over the safety of the abused spouse has misapplied the theology of marriage: God designed marriage for the flourishing of both parties, not for the legal trapping of a victim with their abuser.

verseByVerse.ref: The Gospel for the Abused and the Abuser
verseByVerse.commentary: The gospel speaks to both parties, differently. To the abused person: What is being done to you is wrong. God sees it. He is near to the brokenhearted (Ps. 34:18). His intention for you was never this. You are not trapped by a theology that requires you to remain in danger. Your safety and your children's safety matter to God. To the abuser (separately, with appropriate accountability): What you are doing is sin — serious sin against a person made in God's image, against your covenant vows, against your children, and against God. The gospel offers forgiveness — real forgiveness — and the power of the Spirit to change. But change must be real, sustained, and verified before restoration of the relationship can be considered. Words of repentance are not sufficient; patterns of behavior over time are the evidence.

verseByVerse.ref: The Goal: Protection, Accountability, and Possible Restoration
verseByVerse.commentary: The goal is not divorce — nor is it the preservation of the marriage at any cost. The goal is justice: protection of the vulnerable, accountability for the abuser, and — only if genuine and sustained repentance is demonstrated over a verified period — the possible rebuilding of a relationship on a completely different foundation. Practical steps: (1) Ensure immediate safety — safe housing if necessary, knowledge of legal options. (2) Separate counseling for both parties — never together in the acute phase. (3) For the abuser: a structured accountability process with specific behavioral requirements, involving church elders and potentially legal accountability. (4) For the abused person: pastoral care, practical support, and the rebuilding of their identity in Christ — which the abuser's distorted treatment has typically damaged. (5) Church discipline for the abuser if they are unrepentant (Matt. 18:15–17). Homework for the abused person: identify one safe person you can call if things escalate at home. Write their number in three places. Tell them what is happening.

19.theology:
Submission and safety: The theology of wifely submission (Eph. 5:22–24) has been badly misapplied in domestic abuse situations. The passage must be read in its full context: Ephesians 5:25–33 commands the husband to love his wife as Christ loved the church — sacrificially, self-givingly, as a servant-leader whose exercise of authority looks like laying down his life. The husband who terrorises his wife has not misunderstood submission — he has abandoned the standard to which he is called. No biblical theology of submission requires a woman to remain in a situation of ongoing physical danger.

Church discipline and the abuser: Unrepentant domestic abuse is a matter for church discipline (Matt. 18:15–17). The pastor who applies this faithfully is not destroying a marriage — he is attempting to save a soul. The hope is that the seriousness of formal church discipline will be the wake-up call that produces genuine repentance. But protection of the vulnerable does not wait on that hope.
19.examples:
Then: Abigail (1 Sam. 25) is one of the most remarkable women in Scripture — married to a foolish, cruel man (Nabal), she takes decisive, independent action to protect her household and prevent violence. The narrator presents her wisdom and initiative as entirely appropriate. Her story is a biblical portrait of a woman acting with wisdom and courage to protect those in her care, independently of her husband's authority. The abused woman who acts to protect herself and her children is following a good biblical precedent.

Now: The church must become a place where abused people feel safe enough to tell the truth. This means preaching that names abuse clearly as sin, having trained responders who know how to receive a disclosure, and a culture that does not shame victims or protect powerful abusers. The congregation that has done this work before the crisis arrives will respond faithfully when it does.

20.title: Recommended Literature and Resources
20.overview: Biblical counseling has produced a rich body of literature over the past fifty years. The books listed here are the counselor's essential library — organized by topic, with a note on each. You do not need all of them immediately. Begin with the foundations, then add topic-specific resources as your counseling ministry requires them. All are written from within the biblical counseling tradition and are suitable for use by counselors trained in the ACBC approach.
20.text: "Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety." (Prov. 11:14 ESV) "The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, for the ears of the wise seek it out." (Prov. 18:15 ESV)

verseByVerse.commentary:
Start here:

Paul David Tripp — Instruments in the Redeemer's Hands (P&R, 2002). The single most practical introduction to biblical counseling. Tripp's four-movement model (love, know, speak, do) is accessible, pastoral, and theologically solid. Every biblical counselor should read this first.

Heath Lambert — A Theology of Biblical Counseling (Zondervan, 2016). The most systematic and rigorous theological foundation available. Lambert demonstrates how the doctrines of Scripture, humanity, sin, grace, and sanctification ground the counseling enterprise. Essential for those who want to understand the why behind the how.

David Powlison — Seeing with New Eyes (P&R, 2003). Powlison's collected essays demonstrate the X-ray question method and heart-focused approach at their best. Also: Speaking Truth in Love (New Growth Press) for practical application.

Jay Adams — Competent to Counsel (Zondervan, 1970). The foundational text that started the modern biblical counseling movement. Dated in places, but essential for understanding the tradition's roots and the recovery of the pastoral counseling office.

Tim Lane & Paul Tripp — How People Change (New Growth Press, 2006). The best introductory overview of the change process — how the gospel produces lasting transformation. Excellent for both counselors and counselees.

Brad Bigney — Gospel Treason: Betraying the Gospel with Hidden Idols (P&R, 2012). The most accessible treatment of idol diagnosis. Bigney takes Powlison's and Tripp's insights and makes them immediately applicable. Every counselor and elder should read this.

C.J. Mahaney — Living the Cross Centered Life (Multnomah, 2006). A sustained argument for keeping the cross at the centre of everything — preaching, counseling, parenting, relationships. Mahaney's influence on the ACBC tradition's gospel-centredness is significant.

Tim Keller — Counterfeit Gods (Dutton, 2009). Keller applies idol diagnosis to the most common allegiances — money, sex, power, approval — with cultural sharpness and pastoral warmth. Essential reading for counselors in the contemporary Western context.

Stuart Scott — From Pride to Humility (Focus Publishing, 2002). A short, powerful treatment of pride as the root of most relational conflict. Pairs with Scott's The Exemplary Husband for addressing men's heart issues specifically.

Ed Welch — Running Scared: Fear, Worry, and the God of Rest (New Growth Press, 2007). The finest biblical treatment of anxiety — nuanced, compassionate, deeply practical. Also by Welch: Depression: A Stubborn Darkness (New Growth Press, 2004) — the essential text for counseling depression; Shame Interrupted (New Growth Press, 2012) — for shame and abuse.

Ed Welch — Side by Side: Walking with Others in Wisdom and Love (Crossway, 2015). The best introduction to informal, congregation-level mutual care. Accessible enough for any church member; rich enough for trained counselors.

Martha Peace — The Excellent Wife (Focus Publishing, 1999). The essential text for counseling women in marriage. Also: Damsels in Distress (P&R, 2006) for women's common struggles. Peace's approach is warm, direct, and thoroughly biblical.

Amy Baker — Picture Perfect: When Life Doesn't Line Up (New Growth Press, 2014). Perfectionism, expectations, and the eating disorder connection. Excellent for counseling women struggling with performance-based identity.

Steve Viars — Putting Your Past in Its Place (Harvest House, 2011). For counselees whose past is controlling their present. Viars's approach is practical, structured, and gospel-centred. Also: Loving Your Community (Baker, 2015) for the congregation-level counseling culture.

Heath Lambert — Finally Free: Fighting for Purity with the Power of Grace (Zondervan, 2013). The best gospel-centred treatment of pornography addiction for both counselor and counselee.

Ed Welch — Addictions: A Banquet in the Grave (P&R, 2001). Theologically rigorous and pastorally wise — the essential guide to addiction counseling from a biblical counseling perspective.

David Powlison — How Does Sanctification Work? (Crossway, 2017). Essential for understanding the change process in stubborn or slow-moving situations.

John Street (ed.) — Men Counseling Men (Harvest House, 2012). A comprehensive manual for counseling the specific struggles men face — from anger and addiction to leadership and sexuality. Represents the ACBC tradition's best work for male-specific counseling.

Winston Smith — Marriage Matters (New Growth Press, 2010). For marriage counseling from a biblical counseling perspective.

ACBC Training Resources: The Association of Certified Biblical Counselors (acbc.cc) provides training curricula, conference resources, and a referral network of certified counselors. Certification involves training, examination, and supervised counseling hours — the most rigorous formal training available in the biblical counseling tradition. The Journal of Biblical Counseling (formerly published by CCEF, now available through New Growth Press and online archives) is the movement's flagship academic journal — an invaluable resource for in-depth treatment of specific topics.

CCEF (Christian Counseling and Educational Foundation — ccef.org): Founded by Jay Adams, now home to Ed Welch, David Powlison's archive, and ongoing training. Their online resources, booklets, and courses are among the most practically useful materials available.

20.theology:
The best biblical counselors are people who are always learning — from Scripture, from the tradition's literature, and from every counseling relationship they enter. The books listed here are not substitutes for theological depth, prayerful dependence, and genuine pastoral experience. They are tools in the hands of someone already grounded in the Word of God and committed to the sufficiency of Scripture as the foundation of all soul care.

Randy Patten's vision for the ACBC was a movement of certified counselors embedded in local churches — not a separate profession drawing people away from pastoral care, but an enrichment of it. The well-equipped congregation trains its pastors, elders, and mature members in the principles and skills of biblical counseling, so that the whole body can fulfill Paul's vision in Romans 15:14: 'full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another.'
20.examples:
Reading plan for a new counselor: Year 1 — Tripp's Instruments, Welch's Side by Side, Bigney's Gospel Treason, and Powlison's Seeing with New Eyes. These four books will give you the foundation, the method, the heart diagnosis, and the pastoral posture. Year 2 — add Lambert's Theology of Biblical Counseling, Welch's Running Scared, Depression, and Addictions. Year 3 — specialize according to the specific counseling situations you are encountering most frequently. Every year — the Journal of Biblical Counseling archives, and at minimum one ACBC or CCEF conference or training event.

Finding supervised training: Reading without supervised practice produces knowledgeable but not necessarily effective counselors. Seek out a more experienced biblical counselor who will let you observe, then supervise your sessions, then debrief with you. The ACBC certification process provides a structured framework for this. The best counselors are always under some form of accountability and mentorship — not because they are incompetent, but because the work is too important to do without accountability.
